metadata.author: RevHostHQ
metadata.shortDescription:
You've seen the videos: $10,000 a month, renting cars to rideshare drivers. One host listed the real costs. $400 a week is $1,600 a month. Minus insurance, maintenance, and a reserve for the car you'll lose. That leaves about $300 to $900 a car.
▶ Full lesson, driver-rental checklist and sources: https://www.revhosthq.com/c/66

Rideshare rentals are steady money on hard miles. This lesson covers what they pay, what they cost the car, the insurance gap, and the rule that can get your driver banned.

You'll learn:
• What hosts charge (about $350 to $450 a week, paid in advance) and what drivers put on the car (1,500 to 3,000 miles a week)
• Uber's rule: a rental car has to come through an approved partner, or the driver can be permanently deactivated. Lyft accepts rentals only through its own program
• The insurance gap: the rideshare company covers the driver while the app is on; when it's off, that's on you and the driver
• Why cash and a handshake can get the driver deactivated and leave your car uninsured

Chapters
0:00 $10K a month? One host's real math
0:24 Steady money, hard miles
0:34 What it pays, what it costs the car
0:47 The front door: Uber's and Lyft's rental rules
1:03 The "app off" insurance gap
1:14 Your call: $400 a week, cash
1:38 Sam's checklist before any driver rental
2:02 Rule 6.6 + do this today

RULE 6.6: Rent to drivers only through the front door.
DO THIS TODAY: Read Uber's and Lyft's rental rules for your city, and ask your insurer about the "app off" gap.

Tools mentioned: RevHostHQ, for long-stay renters who aren't driving for an app (weekly and monthly discounts, a deposit hold, and a payment link you resend each week; it doesn't bill renters automatically) → https://www.revhosthq.com/features?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=car-rental-course&utm_content=66

▶ Next lesson, 6.7: Turo and Direct Bookings Together: What Turo Allows and What It Bans → https://youtu.be/-0jEX-skcpc

▶ Free course, every lesson in order: https://www.revhosthq.com/learn/car-rental-business-course

About the numbers: Turo rules and fees are as of October 2026 and can change. Check Turo's help center. "Hosts report" = self-reported by experienced hosts. "One Austin fleet" = real fleet data, shared anonymously. Sam is a fictional worked example.
Not legal, tax, insurance or financial advice.
Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Turo Inc. "Turo" is a trademark of its owner, used here for descriptive purposes only.

metadata.title: I Bought a $5K Car for My Rental Car Business- Here's What It Made
metadata.author: Kel King
metadata.shortDescription:
Can you really make money with a $5,000 car?
In this video, I break down exactly what happened after I bought a $5,000 car and added it to my rental car business. You’ll see the real numbers, what it cost to operate, how much it earned, and whether this business model is actually worth it.

If you’ve ever wanted to start a rental car business, build passive income, or learn how to make money renting cars to Uber & Lyft drivers, this video is for you.

In this video, you’ll learn:
✅ How much a $5,000 car actually made
✅ The real expenses of owning a rental car
✅ How I rent cars to Uber & Lyft drivers
✅ My cash flow and ROI
✅ How to build a profitable rental car business

🚀 Ready to start your own rental car business?
📲 Follow me on Instagram: @rentalcarking

💻 Join My 3-Day Online Car Rental Business Challenge
📅 August 2–4
Learn how to start and scale a profitable rental car business, even if you’re starting with just one car.

🌴 Join Me in Miami for My 3-Day Mastermind
📍 Miami, Florida
📅 August 28–30

Spend three days with me learning the exact systems, strategies, and operations I’ve used to build and grow my rental car business.

👍 If you enjoyed this video, Like, Subscribe, and turn on notifications for weekly content about:

Rental Car Business
Car Rental Business
Passive Income
Entrepreneurship
Fleet Management
Business Systems
Making Money with Cars
💬 Question: If you had $5,000 to invest, would you buy a rental car? Let me know in the comments!

#RentalCarBusiness #CarRentalBusiness #PassiveIncome #UberDriver #Entrepreneur #FleetManagement #SideHustle #CashFlow #Business #FordFusion

🚘 A few years ago I was delivering pizzas and driving regular Uber rides. Today, I’m driving a $125,000 Lincoln Navigator for Uber Black.

Most people told me buying a luxury SUV for Uber was one of the dumbest financial decisions I could make.

In this video, I’m breaking down:

✅ Why I bought a $125,000 SUV

✅ How I got into Uber Black

✅ What it actually costs to operate

✅ The income potential

✅ The risks nobody talks about

✅ Whether I would do it all over again

This isn’t a car review.

This isn’t financial advice.

This is the real story behind one of the biggest financial decisions I’ve ever made.

Would you spend $125,000 on a vehicle if it gave you a chance to level up your life?

Let me know in the comments.

🚘 Uber Black

📈 Business

🎥 YouTube

🌆 Life in NYC

#UberBlack #UberDriver #LincolnNavigator #NYC #Entrepreneurship #EscapeTheMatrix #LuxurySUV #BusinessJourney #FinancialFreedom

Welcome to the channel! In today’s episode, we sit down with CEO Mo from Elevate Car Rentals, who shares his incredible journey from working at a dealership to owning a fleet of over 300 cash cars.
If you’re interested in the rental car business, entrepreneurship, or scaling your side hustle, this conversation is packed with real-world advice, lessons learned, and wild industry stories you won’t want to miss.

metadata.title: How She Turned Cheap Cars Into Weekly Income (Without Turo)
metadata.author: Mr Jay Hill Network
metadata.shortDescription:
FOLLOW YANI ON IG AT @WHIPITWHIPS [ https://www.instagram.com/whipitwhips?igsh=MXFkZ2d3MXozNGd4NQ== ]

Most people think car rental is all about platforms like Turo.
But in this episode, Yani breaks down how she built a private car rental business that generates consistent weekly income — without relying on any platform.
We talk about how she started with just a few cars, realized the limitations of Turo, and built her own system by taking control of her customers, pricing, and marketing.
She explains how she:
turned $5K–$6K cars into weekly cash flow
built demand using simple Google ads
created a waitlist before even having enough cars
rents directly to gig workers like DoorDash and Amazon drivers
scaled her business using partnerships and other people’s cars
uses business funding to grow without using her own money
This isn’t about luxury cars or high-end rentals.
It’s about understanding demand, owning your system, and building a business that actually works.
If you’ve been looking for a real, practical way to create income — this episode breaks it down in a way most people aren’t talking about.

Can you really make money on Turo without doing the work? Jared breaks down how Turo co-hosting allows vehicle owners to earn income from their cars while someone else handles the day-to-day operations—including guest communication, cleaning, vehicle delivery, and managing bookings. metadata.title: I Met Turo Hosts With 400+ Cars… Here’s What They Taught Me
metadata.author: Delano Green
metadata.shortDescription:
I flew to Miami to attend a Turo event and sit down with some of the biggest operators in the car rental space, including people managing fleets of 400+ cars.

What stood out to me most wasn’t just the number of vehicles.

It was how they built the operation, how they manage scale, and how many of these businesses grow without personally owning every single car.

That’s the strategy I’ve been talking about for years:

OPC — Other People’s Cars.

Instead of thinking you need to go into massive debt buying 20, 50, or 100 cars yourself, there’s another model:

Partner with people who already own vehicles, manage those vehicles for them, generate revenue, and split the profits.

In this video, I talk with experienced Turo hosts and fleet operators about:

• Managing hundreds of rental cars
• Scaling beyond owning every vehicle yourself
• Turo co-hosting and fleet management
• Building systems and teams
• Working with vehicle owners
• What actually changes when you go from a few cars to hundreds
• Lessons I can apply to my own rental business
• The future of the Other People’s Cars model

If you're trying to build a rental car business, scale your Turo fleet, or learn how to make money managing vehicles you don't personally own, this video is for you.

Want to learn the OPC Method?

I teach the systems behind acquiring, managing, and profiting from Other People’s Cars.

👉 Grab the free OPC Starter Kit below:
https://whop.com/fleet-launch4u/fleet-launch4u/

Looking to get your car/cars managed and rented on Martha’s Vineyard?

👉 https://mvrentalcars4u.io/turo-fleet-management/

I document what I'm learning while building businesses, managing rental vehicles, interviewing entrepreneurs, and developing the OPC model.

metadata.title: How We Built a 250+ Car Fleet on Turo — Partner Q&A
metadata.author: Philly Car Renting
metadata.shortDescription:
I sat down with my business partner Vadim to answer the questions people ask us about running a Turo fleet: how we started with one personal car in 2020, the money mistake that kills most hosts (depreciation), the stolen car we got back on day 28, our worst buy ever (a Range Rover), and why every single car gets a club, a lockbox, an E-ZPass and a tracker.

We go above and beyond for our guests every day — not with talk, with action. Follow along — we're also building a course and getting ready to go private, and we'll take you through the whole journey.

Chapters:
0:00 How we started: one personal car in 2020
2:51 Turo's shift: power hosts vs mom-and-pop
4:03 The most misunderstood thing about money in Turo
6:32 If a car isn't earning, how fast do we know?
8:31 The stolen car story: recovered on day 28
10:10 Craziest stories: the muffler scam, stolen seats, the lawsuit
12:28 Going private: leaving Turo?
12:58 Have we ever come close to quitting?
15:30 Our worst mistake: the Range Rover
15:58 Why every car gets a club, lockbox, E-ZPass and tracker

Follow us:
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/phillycarrenting
TikTok: https://www.tiktok.com/@philly.turo.car.r

#TuroHost #CarRentalBusiness #FleetLife #TuroTips #PassiveIncome

🚗 Turo Fleet Management / Other People's Cars (OPC)
https://mvrentalcars4u.io/turo-fleet-...

👥 Book a call to learn how to grow your fleet without buying every vehicle yourself.
https://calendly.com/fleetlaunch4u-in...


Here are the key systems I cover in this video:

🚗 Vehicle Onboarding:
 Establishing a consistent process for documenting every vehicle with photos and videos from the moment it joins the fleet.

📋 Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs):
Creating clear, repeatable instructions and training videos for vehicle cleaning, check-ins, inspections, and employee onboarding.

🔑 Key Tracking and Organization:
Labeling vehicle keys, securing spare keys, and ensuring the right keys are available when they're needed.

📅 Reservation Management:
Preparing for upcoming reservations in advance instead of waiting until the day of pickup. The goal is simple: get tomorrow's work done today.

🧼 Cleaning and Inspection Checklists:
Making sure every vehicle is properly cleaned, inspected, and ready for the next guest.

👥 Team Roles and Responsibilities:
Defining ownership of tasks and empowering team members to make decisions within clear guidelines.

⚠️ Damage and Late Return Procedures:
Establishing clear protocols for documenting damage, handling late returns, and responding to unexpected situations.

📍 GPS Monitoring and Vehicle Tracking:
Keeping track of vehicle locations, identifying potential issues, and recognizing which responsibilities still depend too heavily on the owner.

🤝 Vehicle Owner Communication:
Maintaining consistent communication and providing updates to the owners whose vehicles you're managing.

📈 Continuous System Improvement:
Tracking recurring problems, learning from mistakes, and improving processes so the same issues are less likely to happen again.

The biggest lesson? Scaling isn't just about adding more cars. It's about building systems that can handle the complexity that comes with growth.

When your processes are documented, your team understands its responsibilities, and your operations are organized, you can reduce unnecessary mistakes, improve efficiency, and build a business that doesn't depend on you personally handling every task.

Whether you're starting a Turo business, growing your co-hosting operation, or managing vehicles for other people, these systems can help you think differently about scaling your rental business.

𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝘂𝗽 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘁 𝗞𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗙𝗥𝗘𝗘: 


Driving for Uber or Lyft? Before choosing the cheapest car insurance quote, make sure you understand how coverage changes when your app is off, when you're waiting for a ride, and when you've accepted a passenger.

In this video, you'll learn how to compare rideshare insurance options, what a rideshare endorsement may cover, why comprehensive and collision matter, which deductibles and liability limits to compare, and how to use Credit Karma's auto insurance comparison area as a starting point.

You'll also discover what questions to ask insurance companies before purchasing a policy, so you don't accidentally leave yourself exposed while driving for Uber or Lyft.




#RideshareInsurance #UberDriver #LyftDriver #CreditKarma #CarInsurance #Uber #lyft 


𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗿: This video is for educational purposes only and is not insurance, legal, or financial advice. Insurance requirements, availability, limits, exclusions, and deductibles vary by state, insurer, policy, and rideshare platform. Credit Karma may display offers from third-party providers; availability and terms vary. Confirm your rideshare use and all coverage details directly with a licensed insurer or agent before purchasing.

metadata.title: Commercial Auto Insurance for Side Hustles (LLCs & Uber)
metadata.author: The Finance Blueprint
metadata.shortDescription:
Video Description

Starting a side hustle or an LLC is an exciting way to build wealth, but many entrepreneurs are unknowingly driving around with a "ticking time bomb" in their glovebox. In this video, we dive deep into why your personal auto insurance policy likely excludes your business activities—and how one accident could bankrupt your LLC and your personal savings.

We break down the specific benefits of **Progressive Commercial Auto Insurance**, the "Three Periods" of rideshare coverage, and why a Certificate of Insurance (COI) is the key to landing bigger, more profitable contracts. Don't let an "insurance gap" destroy years of hard work. Learn how to protect your hustle, your vehicle, and your future.

---

Timestamps & Chapters

*   **0:00** – The Insurance Nightmare: A Real-World Scenario
*   **1:15** – The LLC Trap: Why Your "Shield" Might Be Broken
*   **2:30** – Personal vs. Commercial Risk: Understanding Exclusions
*   **3:45** – The 3 Periods of Rideshare (Uber, Lyft, DoorDash)
*   **5:10** – Liability Limits: How to Prevent Your Assets from Being Seized
*   **6:40** – Protecting Your Gear: Coverage for Tools & Cargo
*   **8:00** – The Real Cost: Is Commercial Insurance Actually Expensive?
*   **9:15** – Snapshot ProView & Multi-Policy Discounts
*   **10:30** – The Rideshare Endorsement vs. Full Commercial Policies
*   **11:50** – Uninsured Motorist Coverage: Protecting Your Income
*   **13:10** – The Entity Factor: Titling Your Vehicle Correctly
*   **14:40** – Scaling Up: How a COI (Certificate of Insurance) Opens Doors
*   **16:00** – How to Switch: Getting a Quote the Right Way
*   **17:30** – Conclusion: Building a Business That Actually Lasts

---

Key Takeaways from this Video
*   **The Insurance Gap:** Why personal policies void your coverage the moment you're "on the clock."
*   **Asset Protection:** How Progressive's $1M Combined Single Limit (CSL) protects your business better than split-limit personal policies.
*   **Inland Marine Insurance:** How to insure cameras, tools, and catering equipment that your standard policy ignores.
*   **Tax Benefits vs. Risk:** Why titling a car in your LLC name requires a commercial policy.

#SideHustle #LLC #ProgressiveInsurance #CommercialAuto #GigEconomy #UberDriver #SmallBusinessTips #FinanceEducation

metadata.title: How I Installed a Goldstar GPS Tracker and Kill Switch In My Rental Car Fleet
metadata.author: Pitstop to Profits
metadata.shortDescription:
Stop paying $200–$300 to get GPS trackers and kill switches installed on your rental fleet or personal vehicles! In this video, I break down exactly how to wire up a Spireon GoldStar GPS tracker and a starter-interrupt kill switch on a Kia Sportage in under an hour using basic tools.

Whether you manage an independent car rental company, host on Turo, or just want to secure your daily driver against theft, this step-by-step walkthrough shows you how simple it is to protect your assets yourself and save serious money.

What You’ll Learn in This Video:

The basic, budget-friendly tools you need (under $100 total)

How to install just the 3-wire GPS tracker (Constant 12V, Switched Ignition Sense, and Ground)

How to use a multimeter to test the main ignition switch harness without guessing

How to wire the starter disable relay so you can remotely disable the vehicle

How to read basic electrical schematics to verify your ignition lines

Timestamps / Video Chapters:
0:00 - Intro & Stop Overpaying for Tracker Installs
0:58 - What Comes in the GoldStar Tracker & Kill Switch Kit
2:24 - Budget Tools You Need (Multimeter & Wire Strippers)
3:55 - The 3 Core Wires for Tracker-Only Installs
5:50 - Testing & Verifying 12V Constant Power with a Multimeter
7:58 - Testing the Switched Ignition Sense Wire
9:11 - Securing the Chassis Ground & Checking GPS/Cell Signals
10:23 - Step-by-Step Starter Kill Relay Wiring
11:42 - Slicing the Ignition Starter Line & Making Connections
13:20 - Summary & Clean Installation Recap
14:14 - Reading Vehicle Wiring Schematics (O'Reilly Trick)
15:53 - Final Thoughts & Outro

Core Connections Breakdown:

Chassis Ground (Black): Bare metal chassis ground

Constant 12V (Red with Fuse): Tapped to the unswitched 12V constant line on the ignition harness (reads 12V with key OFF)

Ignition Sense (White): Tapped to switched ignition line (reads 0V OFF, 12V+ in ON/RUN)

Relay Signal (Green to Green): Connects relay harness directly to the GPS tracker

Starter Interrupt Cut (Red/White from Relay): Splices across the cut factory starter crank wire

Discussion Question:
Pit crew: Are you installing your own GPS trackers and kill switches or paying a shop? Drop your thoughts, questions, or fleet setup in the comments below!

Subscribe to the channel for more straight-talk fleet management advice, business systems, and automotive DIY walkthroughs.

segments.text: Today I'm checking out Bouncy, the GPS
tracker that plugs into your car's OBD2
port and sends live driving data right
to your phone. I've been using it for a
while, so this review is based on real
use, not just a first impression. Once
you set it up, the app starts showing
your vehicle's location, speed, trip
details, and even alerts for things like
hard braking or rapid acceleration.
Setup is simple. Plug it in, connect
through Bluetooth, and link it to the
bouncy mobile app. The app interface
looks clean and updates every 15
seconds, which is fast compared to some
other trackers. You can see routes in
detail with each trip logged
automatically. It also tracks mileage
and shows fuel levels if your car
supports it. The trip history feature is
useful if you want to review past routes
or see how efficiently you've been
driving. But not everything works
perfectly. Sometimes the location data
lags or shows a delay when your car
moves. It's not a huge issue, but worth
noting if you need realtime precision.
The app also requires a paid
subscription, so even though the device
itself is affordable, you'll have
ongoing monthly costs. The support
section is decent, but responses can
take a day or two. Bouncy does send
alerts to your phone for events like
speeding or if your car moves
unexpectedly. This is helpful if you
share a car or have a teen driver. The
driving insights are detailed enough to
help you build safer habits, and you can
export reports if you want to track
usage for business. In my honest
opinion, Bouncy is a solid option if you
want an easy to use tracker with
consistent performance. It's not
perfect. Sometimes updates lag and the
subscription might be annoying, but
overall, it delivers what it promises.
I'd recommend it for families, small
business owners, or anyone who just
wants peace of mind about where their
car is and how it's being driven. If you
found this review useful, hit the like
button and subscribe for more honest
tech reviews.

metadata.title: You Can STILL Make $300-$500 a Day Driving Uber Black
metadata.author: TJackk
metadata.shortDescription:
Yes, you can still make $300–$500 a day driving Uber Black — but you have to know how to work the market.

In this video, I react to one of my own morning shifts where I made $275 in under 6 hours and break down exactly what I did, including starting at 4AM, targeting business and airport traffic, and keeping the wheels moving instead of sitting around waiting on only Black rides.

Join the Uber Black Fleet Community for step-by-step videos, resources, templates, and an inside look at how I operate my fleet:

https://whop.com/joined/luxury-driver-network/products/uber-black-fleet-community/


If you need more hands-on help getting started, I also offer multiple mentorship options here:

https://shop.beacons.ai/tjackk/eaff5f54-b512-477e-8151-f6aecac723d9


Subscribe to TJackk for new videos:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCNK0Rhs_FIjKmMIGaoQFmHQ

Follow TJackk:
https://www.instagram.com/tjackkhustle/
https://www.facebook.com/p/TJackk-100064811620961/

#UberBlack #UberDriver #UberBlackDriver #RideshareTips #UberEarnings #AirportRides #RideshareDriver #UberStrategy #BlackCarService #TJackk

metadata.title: Fast Track Mobility Enters NYC’s TLC Plate Rental Market as Drivers Seek Flexible Ownership Options
metadata.author: AutoMarketplace
metadata.shortDescription:
NYC TLC fleet Fast Track Mobility is launching a driver-centric plate rental program that lets TLC-licensed drivers use their own vehicles while renting a TLC plate bundled with insurance coverage.

*LINKS*

Fast Track TLC Plate Rentals: https://fasttrackleasingllc.com/plate-rental-apply/

AutoMarketplace Newsletter: https://automarketplace.com/newsletter

*TABLE OF CONTENTS*

00:00 – Introduction
02:21 – What is a NYC TLC Plate rental?
05:23 – Who is renting TLC Plates? What’s driving demand?
08:28 – What does a Fast Track TLC Plate rental cost? What about insurance?
09:29 – Fast Track’s unique TLC insurance offering
10:25 – Pricing breakdown: $115/week (TLC Plate + DMV registration), $174/week (TLC insurance) = $289/week total (~$1,250/month)
12:32 – More details on TLC Plate rental terms: $1,000 deposit, 56-week contract
14:16 – Individual (peer-to-peer) vs. corporate TLC Plate rentals
18:38 – Title technicalities: Fast Track listed as DMV co-registrant
20:44 – It takes 4–6 weeks to receive a title after purchasing a vehicle
22:50 – Step 1: Driver buys a vehicle and obtains the title
23:30 – Step 2: Fast Track background check and insurance pre-approval
23:45 – What if the vehicle title is not in the driver’s name?
24:02 – Can a driver check insurance eligibility before buying a vehicle?
24:41 – Step 3: Making and attending an in-person Fast Track appointment — vehicle inspection, required documents, $500 deposit, vehicle drop-off
27:00 – Fast Track installs a GPS tracker (non-immobilizing)
27:39 – Dash camera requirements
28:02 – Step 4: Fast Track sends a text message with the NY DMV FS-6 form confirming the return of the vehicle’s regular plates, allowing drivers to cancel prior insurance; Fast Track then submits the DMV application to attach its TLC plates
29:27 – Step 5: Fast Track notifies TLC, waits for inspection, and collects the final $500 deposit payment at vehicle pickup
30:10 – How long does the process take? (4–6 weeks) Can drivers take their own vehicles to the TLC inspection?
31:18 – When do weekly TLC Plate payments begin?
31:50 – Quick summary of all TLC Plate rental steps and timeline (why 4–6 weeks? Why a $1,000 deposit?)
35:30 – Can drivers attach Fast Track TLC Plates to gas-powered (ICE), hybrid, or EV vehicles?
36:11 – 56-week contract terms, 6-week cancellation notice, deposit return policy
37:45 – Is Fast Track exiting the TLC vehicle rental business? How many TLC Plates are available?
39:45 – TLC insurance clarifications (liability vs. comprehensive and collision coverage)
41:35 – Gaming out future TLC Plate releases, EV rules, and auto loan considerations
44:05 – Concluding thoughts

metadata.title: $37.44/Hour: How to Become an Uber Driver in New York City (2026)
metadata.author: Paydirt
metadata.shortDescription:
According to Uber's own data, NYC drivers average about $37.44 an hour — the highest rideshare pay of any city in America. This video breaks down realistic NYC earnings, the TLC license you must have first, and exactly how to get on the road.

How to get started:
1. Get your TLC license: apply through the NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission, complete a medical exam and drug test, get fingerprinted, and finish the 24-hour TLC driver course (~$627–827 total, 4–8 weeks).
2. Sign up to drive at the official Uber driver site.
3. Get a TLC-plated vehicle — your own car with TLC plates, or rent from a TLC rental company.
4. Pass Uber's background screening and upload your documents.
5. Go online and start accepting rides.

Pro tips: learn the JFK and LaGuardia airport game, own the weekend late nights in Manhattan when surge peaks, and watch the cost side — congestion pricing, tolls, and parking tickets eat earnings fast. Note: pay figures are gross; you cover gas, maintenance, depreciation, and commercial TLC insurance, plus ~15.3% self-employment tax and New York State + New York City income taxes.

Links & guides:
- Sign up to drive with Uber (official): https://drivers.uber.com
- NYC TLC driver licensing (official): https://www.nyc.gov/tlc

Disclaimer: This video is for informational purposes only and is not financial advice. Earnings figures are estimates based on published third-party data and will vary by market, hours worked, and effort. Do your own research before making any decisions.

New York is genuinely in a league of its

Limousine Commission sets minimum pay
standards for app-based drivers, which
gives you a legal floor under your
earnings that drivers in most cities do
not have. Now, the gate. To drive Uber
or Lyft anywhere in New York City, you
need a TLC license from the Taxi and
Limousine Commission. It is illegal to
carry passengers for hire without one.
Here's how to get it.
Step one, submit your application
through the TLC's online system.
Step two, complete a medical exam and a
drug test.
Step three, get fingerprinted for a
background check.
Step four, complete the 24-hour TLC
driver course and pass the exam.
The whole process takes about four to
eight weeks and costs roughly 600 to 800
dollars all in.
You also need a regular New York
driver's license that you you held for
at least one year. Step five, sign up to
drive at the official Uber driver site.
Step six, get your vehicle. It must be
TLC plated, which means either your own
car with TLC plates or a rental from one
of the many TLC rental companies in the
city.
Many new drivers rent at first to test
the waters before buying.
Step seven, pass Uber's background
screening, upload your documents, and go
online. Here are three tips tailored to
New York City.
First, learn the airport game.
JFK and LaGuardia runs are the bread and
butter of New York rideshare. Know the
terminals, know the pickup lots, and
position yourself near the airports
during arrival banks.
Second, own the weekend late nights.
Manhattan on a Friday or Saturday night,
when the subways slow down and the bars
let out, is when surge pricing does its
best work.
Third, respect the cost side. Congestion
pricing, tolls, and parking tickets can
quietly eat your earnings.
Plan your positioning so you're not
idling in traffic, and never leave a car
double parked while you wait for a
rider.
One ticket can wipe out a whole shift.
One honest caveat before you jump in.
That $37.44 is gross pay, not take home.
You cover gas, maintenance,
depreciation, and commercial-grade TLC
insurance, which is far more expensive
than a personal policy.
You owe roughly 15% in self-employment
tax on top of income tax, and remember
that New York State and New York City
both levy their own income taxes.
Track every mile, every toll, and every
expense. A simple mileage log can save
you thousands at tax time.
That is Uber in New York City, the
highest rideshare pay in the country,
behind a license that takes a month or
two to earn.

metadata.title: 🔐🚖 NYC TLC Plate (FHV License) Storage: Step-by-Step Guide for Drivers & Fleets
metadata.author: AutoMarketplace
metadata.shortDescription:
No one wants to lose their NYC TLC Plates (a/k/a FHV License). However, sometimes circumstances make it difficult to keep up with the associated administration and expenses, such as insurance. For example, your TLC-plated vehicle might be involved in an accident, require major repairs, or you may need to travel abroad for a couple of months.

This is why the TLC created a 90 day FHV License (TLC Plate) Storage Program, which permits licensees to put their current FHV license in storage once every 2-year renewal period for up to 90 consecutive days (https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/vehicles/for-hire-vehicle-license-storage.page).

The process can be a bit complicated to understand, so we've created a step-by-step guide on how to:

1. Store your NYC TLC Plates (FHV License)
2. How to remove your NYC TLC Plates from the FHV License Storage Program

*TABLE OF CONTENTS*

0:00 Intro
0:27 Making sure your TLC Plates can be stored
1:45 TLC UP - https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/tlc-online/tlc-up.page
3:28 DMV Plate Surrender (FS-6)
4:56 *STORING* your NYC TLC Plates
5:34 Notify your TLC insurance broker
6:00 Important disclaimer
6:22 *REMOVING* your TLC Plates from storage
6:50 Step 1: Contact a TLC insurance broker (https://automarketplace.com/)
7:15 Documents to gather
8:00 Step 2: Double check new TLC insurance pages
8:15 Step 3: TLC UP process (submitting Plate *&* Vehicle transfer) - https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/tlc-online/tlc-up.page)
9:55 Step 4: Making TLC transfer (and/or license renewal) payments - https://apps.nyc.gov/lars/
11:42 Step 5: Receiving a DMV Plate Letter from TLC
12:31 Step 6: Getting your new TLC Pates from DMV
12:46 DMV appointment needs to be in NYC
13:12 Step 7: Notifying TLC of new DMV TLC Plates - https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/tlc-online/tlc-up.page)
13:51 Step 8: Attending and passing TLC inspection
14:28 Need help? (https://automarketplace.com/)

*LINKS*

NYC TLC For-Hire Vehicle License Storage: https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/vehicles/for-hire-vehicle-license-storage.page

NYC TLC UP: https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/tlc-online/tlc-up.page

metadata.title: What It Really Takes to Run a Million-Dollar Car Rental Business
metadata.author: Russ Unlocked
metadata.shortDescription:
A real look behind the scenes of running and growing a private car rental business.

This vlog is about more than just cars — it’s the business, the decisions, the relationships, the systems, and the lifestyle that come with building a fleet and creating something that can scale.

A lot of people see the cars, the money, and the freedom.

What they don’t always see is the work behind it.

That’s what this channel is about.

If you’re interested in private car rentals, entrepreneurship, fleet building, business growth, and seeing what the journey actually looks like behind the scenes, subscribe and follow along.

Instagram: @russunlocked

Filmed by: @mike.envisions

#CarRentalBusiness #PrivateCarRental #Entrepreneurship #EntrepreneurVlog #FleetBusiness #RussUnlocked

metadata.title: 🤔🐆🎙️ NYC TLC Leasing: "Predatory" Business Model (?), Plates, EVs & More
metadata.author: AutoMarketplace
metadata.shortDescription:
AutoMarketplace Founder Dawood Mian sits down with three local NYC entrepreneurs who run TLC fleet leasing companies to speak about their businesses, how they think about the market (i.e., TLC Plates, EVs, regulations) and their thoughts on constantly being called "predatory".

**************
TABLE OF CONTENTS:

👋 00:00 - Intro
🧑 00:49 - Background of NYC TLC fleet owners
🚕 06:35 - Why do we need NYC TLC leasing companies? What's the value?
😧 11:29 - Biggest issues TLC leasing companies face
😬 15:27 - Real life examples of issues faced
👩‍🔧 19:45 - Physical damage & collision (self-insurance)
🤷 27:18 - Why are people paying $500 per week for a Camry?
🤑 36:18 - NYC TLC leasing profit margins?
🛑 37:50 - 60 day non-use Summons (JW TLC summons)
😩 41:52 - GM (Maven), Lyft (Flexdrive) experience in NYC TLC leasing business
🗣️ 43:23- Talking NYC TLC Plates
🤔 46:15 - Why is there a TLC Plate Cap? Impact on leasing business?
🧠 49:30 - Understanding driver business mentality 
💰 52:45 - What are TLC Plates (FHV Corp) worth? Have you bought TLC Plates (FHV Corp)? Why? 
🚖 1:00:40 - NYC TLC Plate (FHV Corp) vs. NYC Taxi Medallion
🐆 1:06:12 - "Predatory" accusation against TLC leasing companies
⚡ 1:17:48 - EV exemption to TLC Plate Cap? Using EVs for TLC work?
🗽 1:27:49 - Thoughts on regulation in the NYC TLC market & EVs
💸 1:33:27 - New EV TLC Plates impact on drivers earnings
⚖️ 1:35:35 - TLC regulation is pushing businesses to edge & need for public hearing
⚡ 1:37:57 - What if TLC opens up EV TLC Plates again?
👋 1:42:28 - Final thoughts

**************

*OTHER LINKS*
AutoMarketplace Newsletter Link: https://automarketplace.substack.com/p/nyc-tlc-leasing-predatory-business

#nyctaxi #ubernyc #tlcplates

Welcome to Business Rocket! In this video, Alex breaks down everything you need to know about obtaining a TCP license, focusing specifically on vehicle requirements. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) manages TCP licenses, and surprisingly, there are no strict vehicle requirements. However, your vehicle must be commercially registered, indicating its dedicated use for business purposes.

Visit our website for more information about the TCP License: https://www.businessrocket.com/get/california-tcp-license-registration/

Discover key insights on selecting the right vehicle for your TCP license. Alex delves into the significant considerations, including insurance costs and vehicle suitability for specific services. Learn how insurance premiums vary based on vehicle type and usage frequency, and why aligning your vehicle choice with service provider preferences can boost your chances of success in the industry.

Whether you're looking to get a TCP license, register a vehicle, or understand what a TCP license entails, this video provides invaluable guidance. Don't miss out on expert tips to streamline your journey into the transportation business.

Got questions? Drop them in the comments below, and we'll ensure you receive prompt answers. Stay tuned for more insightful content from Business Rocket. Start your journey towards a successful TCP license today!

#TCPLicense #VehicleRequirements #GetTCPLicense #RegisterTCPLicense #TCPVehicle #BusinessRocket #Entrepreneurship #TransportationBusiness #CPUC #InsuranceCosts #CommercialRegistration


Video Transcript: 

Hello, um, my fellow entrepreneurs. It's Alex from Business rocket. And today we're going to discuss the TCP license, specifically vehicle requirements. Now, the TCP license and the CPUC who manages the TCP license does not have a vehicle requirement at all. So you can actually register any vehicle you want to be on your TCP license.

The only requirement there is, is to make sure that that vehicle is commercially registered, meaning that you went to the DMV, you've presented them with a weight certificate, and you asked the DMV to change the registration of your vehicle to commercial use, meaning that the car is being used for business purposes only and not personal purposes.

Once that's done, you can add that vehicle to the TCP license. But there's two things you want to consider when you're actually picking a vehicle. Number one is the cost of insurance. Uh, insurance can be extremely expensive, and it actually depends on the type of vehicle you have. So the more common the vehicle and the more likely that it's going to be on the road a lot, the more expensive the insurance is going to be.

Sometimes more expensive vehicles, but the vehicles that are not going to be used a lot, like a stretch limousine or a shuttle bus, uh, like a sprinter van, those can have cheaper insurances than, for example, a Prius or a sedan. So you want to kind of talk to an insurance broker and find out, once you've identified the vehicle that you want to get, how much that insurance would be and how is it different from maybe a different vehicle that you wanted to get.

Number two, when you're picking a vehicle, you want to figure out what the vehicle is for. So, for example, before you even start looking at vehicles, contact vendors like Uber or Lyft, or maybe a, uh, third party vendor you're planning to work with and find out what vehicles they want.

Because if you get a car that they want, they're more likely to hire you. We've seen this happen a lot where people just randomly buy a car and think they can add it because it looks nice. But I can promise you that they don't care how nice it looks.

If it doesn't go into their parameters, they'll decline the car, and you're going to have to spend all that money to buy a new car and sell this car. And the process needs to be kind of restarted. So hopefully this video is very helpful. If you have any questions, leave it below.

We'll get you answers right away, and I look forward to speaking to you in the future. Have a great day.

metadata.author: Luxury Transportation Academy / Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to Episode 1 of The Luxury Transportation Podcast! 🚘

In this premiere episode, host Durrell Willis sits down with Dr. Morris Parker — CEO of TCW Limo and founder of the Luxury Transportation Academy (LTA) — to break down what it really takes to build a successful luxury transportation business from the ground up.

From landing his first celebrity client in 2013 to building a multi-vehicle operation generating over $200K/year, Dr. Parker shares the mindset, systems, and day-to-day workflow behind running a top-tier chauffeur service.

🎙️ In this episode, we cover:
✅ How Dr. Morris Parker got started in the limo industry
✅ Why customer value & relationships drive repeat business
✅ The importance of using the right software & tech stack
✅ A real day-in-the-life of a luxury transportation company
✅ Black car service vs. rideshare/taxi — what sets luxury apart
✅ The $100K-per-vehicle blueprint to scale your fleet
✅ Why mentorship through LTA can fast-track your success

Whether you're an aspiring chauffeur, a startup black car operator, or a seasoned limo company owner looking to scale, this episode is packed with actionable insights to elevate your business.

📌 Learn more about the Luxury Transportation Academy and start building your roadmap to success today.

👉 Subscribe for new episodes every week!

#LuxuryTransportation #BlackCarService #ChauffeurLife #LimoBusiness #EntrepreneurPodcast #TCWLimo #LTAAcademy #GroundTransportation #SmallBusinessGrowth #LuxuryTransportationPodcast

metadata.title: The Economics of Running an Uber Fleet
metadata.author: Owners Risk
metadata.shortDescription:
You don't rent cars to Uber drivers. You rent access to a marketplace where the platform sets the rider's price, sets the driver's pay, and can change either number without asking you.

This video breaks down what it actually costs to run an Uber fleet — from the four different tiers of the business, to vehicle acquisition costs, to the hidden insurance and licensing fees that vary wildly by city. It walks through the real per-vehicle math on how fleet income is layered, and the structural vulnerability at the center of the whole model: you own the car, but you don't own the pricing algorithm. It uses the collapse of the New York taxi medallion, a license that once traded for over a million dollars and now sells for a fraction of that, to show what happens when a platform makes the old monopoly irrelevant. It also covers where the industry is actually heading, as fleet operators shift toward managing depots for autonomous vehicle companies instead of renting cars to human drivers at all. The video closes with an honest good-year, bad-year comparison for a five-car fleet, using real dollar figures.

Every business looks simple from the outside. We show you the fine print.

#economics #financeexplained #uberdriver #uber

The National Employment Law Project measured it at roughly 42% by the end of 2024, up from 32% before Uber introduced its current pricing [music] system. Princeton's Workers Algorithm Observatory, studying Oregon Trip data, calculated actual take rates of 44% for Uber and 52% [music] for Lyft. Whatever the true number is, average weekly driver earnings fell from $531 [music] to $513 for Uber drivers between 2023 [music] and 2024. And Lyft drivers saw a 14% drop over the same period. None of that is something a fleet [music] owner controls. You own the car. Uber owns the pricing model that determines whether your car [music] earns enough for the driver to afford your rental fee this week. That vulnerability is the [music] entire New York medallion story. The medallion was supposed to be the moat, a government-capped [music] monopoly that made the license itself a retirement plan. Then a platform arrived that didn't need a medallion at all. And it didn't just compete, it collapsed the asset [music] by roughly 90% within half a decade. Dorothy Lacant drove a yellow cab in New York for over 35 years and went on hunger strike fighting for [music] debt relief only to have her private lender demand an immediate $130,000 cash payment she couldn't pay. Wilfred Extanis, a 64year-old driver, had his medallion repeatedly repossessed during the pandemic [music] by a lender that refused to join the city's relief program. Richard Chow's younger brother, Kenny Chow, took his own life in [music] 2018 under more than $600,000 of medallion debt. New York eventually built the Medallion [music] Relief Program Plus, writing loan balances that averaged $550,000 to $750,000 down to $200,000 with a $30,000 city grant reducing the real debt to $170,000 [music] financed over 25 years. By January 2023, that program had delivered $356 million in forgiveness across [music] 1,789 medallions before closing to new applicants in April 2024. Between 250 and 400 drivers [music] were still excluded because a handful of private lenders simply refused to participate. Zoom out and the macro force reshaping this entire industry is autonomous vehicles. As of mid2025, Whimo is running roughly 400,000 paid rides a week across 11 US [music] cities on pace to cross a million weekly rides before the end of 2026. In September 2024, [music] Uber and Whimo announced an expanded partnership launching in Austin and Atlanta, where Uber dispatches [music] Whimo self-driving cars directly through its own app. And Uber itself [music] handles the physical fleet work, cleaning, repairs, depot operations, while Whimo handles the driving software. Uber's CEO has said publicly that for [music] the next decade, humans and machines will run side by side. But that by 2040, robot drivers will be safer and cheaper than human ones, and human driving will [music] become a niche, recreational activity rather than a job. That's not a distant [music] hypothetical for a fleet operator. It's the reason Avis signed a multi-year deal in [music] July 2025 to become Whimo's primary fleet operations partner in Dallas, managing depots and vehicle readiness instead of renting cars to human drivers at all. And that's the honest answer to why serious well- capitalized players are still moving into this space even knowing everything above. They're not [music] betting on the driver rental model long term. They're positioning to become the physical operations layer underneath a robo taxi network, a stable corporate [music] services contract instead of a volatile consumer leasing business. That's a fundamentally different [music] business than renting a Camry to a driver for $300 a week. And it's the version [music] of this industry that actually looks durable. Now, the honest math for the business most people are actually picturing. Goodyear, a fivecar fleet. Standard weekly rental model, $1,500 [music] gross fairs per vehicle, 25% Uber commission. Driver keeps [music] $900, you net $225 per vehicle per week. That's $4,500 a [music] month, roughly $54,000 a year against maybe $150,000 in vehicle capital and standard market insurance and [music] maintenance costs of $3,100 to $4,750 per car annually. Modest, but real. Bad year. Same five cars, but you're operating in New York. Congestion pricing launched the 5th of January, 2025, adding a $1.50 [music] 50 cents per trip searchcharge on top of existing fees, pushing total ride share search charges to $4.25 [music] a trip before the fair even starts. A study of TLC data found total highvolume rid share trips fell nearly 6% after the toll launched and shared [music] rides specifically collapsed by over 38%. On top of that, platforms had spent 20024 quietly locking drivers out of the app during slow hours to [music] avoid minimum pay rules, meaning your rented cars sat idle midshift with no driver able to log in and no fair coming in until the TLC finally banned the practice in June 2025. Your insurance alone in this market runs $7,500 to $15,000 [music] per vehicle a year instead of $2,500. Utilization drops, fairs drop, and your fixed costs, the ones tied to owning the car, not to how much it's driven, don't move at all, on the same fivecar fleet. In that environment, you're not clearing $54,000. [music] You're closer to breaking even or losing money once a single vehicle needs an unplanned repair. The gap between those two years was never about how hard you worked or how well you maintained the cars. It was set by an algorithm you'll never see. Running on a platform that can lock [music] your driver out of his own shift with 72 hours notice. In a business where the license used to be [music] the safest asset in America until the day it wasn't. You bought the cars, you own the metal, but the row of vehicles sitting in that lot was never really your business. It was always Ubers.

metadata.title: Best Cars for Rideshare Drivers: Hybrid Edition
metadata.author: The Rideshare CEO
metadata.shortDescription:
You have seen all three of these cars before, on earlier lists. So let us be honest up front. This video is not three new cars. It is the class comparison. Same hybrid power, three different shapes, and the shape decides what job the car can actually do for you.

A compact hatchback, a Comfort sedan, and an SUV do not compete with each other. They fit different drivers. So we rank them by how many rideshare jobs each shape can cover.

CHAPTERS:
00:00 The class comparison — same hybrid power, three shapes
01:06 #3 Toyota Prius — efficiency king, compact shape
03:20 #2 Toyota Camry Hybrid — the Comfort sedan shape
05:38 #1 Toyota RAV4 Hybrid — the SUV shape that does it all
08:22 The recap — pick by the job

Why the RAV4 wins: 40 mpg combined, Comfort eligible, and 37.6 cubic feet of cargo behind the seats — four passengers plus airport luggage actually fits. It burns the most fuel here, but it covers the most jobs.

Why the Camry is #2: 51 mpg (LE hybrid), the benchmark Comfort sedan, a hybrid battery covered 10 years / 150,000 miles on 2020 and newer models, and a 250,000–300,000+ mile lifespan.

Why the Prius is #3: 57 mpg (Gen 5 LE) — the best fuel economy here — and the cheapest miles of any car in this video. But it tops out at UberX and Green in most markets. No Comfort. That is a structural earnings ceiling.

Pick by the job, not by the badge. City-only, high miles, lowest cost per mile: take the Prius. Airport runs and Comfort fares in a sedan: take the Camry Hybrid. Comfort, luggage, and clearance in one car: take the RAV4 Hybrid.

Comfort and XL lists are per city and tighten by model year — check your city's list in the driver app before you buy. That is the final word.

All prices, MPG, warranties, and traps in this video come from our October 2026 research dossiers for the original 14-car countdown. Prices move — verify before you buy.

#Rideshare #UberDriver #LyftDriver #BestCarsForRideshare #ToyotaPrius #ToyotaCamry #ToyotaRAV4 #HybridCars

metadata.title: How To Start A Car Rental Business in 2026 WITHOUT Cars | On Consignment
metadata.author: Etienne Elsaesser
metadata.shortDescription:
Start your own Car Rental Business in less than 60 days: https://go.toptierrentalmastery.com/ca3aadd8

Most car rental operators think they need more cash, better credit, or more financing to grow. But the real way to scale a rental fleet is not always buying more cars it is learning how to manage other people’s assets professionally.

In this video, I break down the exact consignment pitch I used to bring exotic and luxury cars into my fleet without buying them, financing them, or putting my own capital at risk. At one point, 55 vehicles in my fleet were consignment cars, generating serious monthly revenue while the owners kept their assets and shared in the upside.

You’ll learn:

- Why car rental is really an asset management business
- What wealthy exotic car owners actually care about
- How to open the conversation without sounding desperate
- The financial math that makes consignment obvious
- Where to find exotic car owners who may be open to deals
- What contract terms protect both sides
- How to scale from a few cars to a real rental fleet without using only your own money

This is not legal or tax advice. Always speak with a lawyer and CPA before structuring consignment agreements.

Would you use this consignment strategy to grow your car rental fleet?

#CarRentalBusiness
#ExoticCarRental
#LuxuryCarRental

segments.text: We had 55 rental cars in my fleet that
we didn't pay a single dollar for. No
financing, no down payment, no
[clears throat] partner buying, nothing.
The owners handed me the keys, signed a
contract, and walked away. And those
same cars were generating $150,000
a revenue that we split with the owners.
And this is called consignment. And the
reason most operators never use it is
not because rich people don't want to do
it. It's because most operators don't
know how to ask. In the next 15 minutes,
I'm going to break down exactly the
pitch that I used to get exotic car
owners to hand me over their six-figure
[music] exotic vehicles for free. The
math that makes them say yes before I
even finish talking. And the one
financial argument that flips a no into
a where do I sign almost every single
time. If you're trying to grow a car
rental fleet right now, and you've been
telling yourself, "I can't grow because
of my capital or financial or credit
situation," this video is going to
change how you think about the entire
business. Here's the part that most
rental operators get wrong from day one.
They think that the rental business is a
car business. It's not. It's an asset
management business that just so happens
to use cars. Once you understand that,
everything starts to change. Because in
the asset management world, nobody is
buying their own assets. Hedge funds
don't own the money that they invest.
They manage other people's money. Real
estate fund managers don't actually own
the buildings. They manage other
people's buildings. Private equity firms
don't fund their own deals. They raise
capital from people who already have it.
Why? Because using your own capital is
the slowest way you're going to grow
your business. If you put $200,000
into one Lamborghini, you have one
Lamborghini. If you take that same
prove you can operate a fleet
professionally, and then use it as
leverage to bring on consignment
vehicles, you can be running five to 10
cars within your first [music] year.
Same capital, five to 10 times the
revenue. And without the depreciation
risk on cars you don't own. That's the
entire game. And once you see it, you
simply cannot unsee it. The operators
stuck at one or two cars are the ones
that are still trying to buy their way
to scaling. The operators running real
fleets figured out how to get other
people to fund their inventory. Before
we go deeper, let me tell you about why
I'm the one who's talking about this.
I've been operating a rental fleet for
over eight years. We've run up to 60
vehicles, about half of them being
exotic and half of them being economy
cars, managed remotely with an
on-the-ground operations team who
handles pickups, drop-offs, inspections,
and anything else that we need. Of those
60 cars, about 55 of them were
consignment vehicles, meaning I don't
own them, I didn't finance them, I have
absolutely zero money tied up in them. I
just operate them, take a split of the
revenue, and the owner takes the rest.
I've also worked with over 20 operators
in the country to help them scale their
own fleet using the same model. People
like Ed, who went from having about five
cars to having 15 cars on the fleet,
with 10 of them being consignment
vehicles. And we did that within just a
short two-month time frame. And his cars
are luxury and exotic vehicles. I'm
telling you this so you know that this
system is not just theory. It's been
deployed against actual six-figure and
multiple six-figure vehicles with actual
high net-worth owners in actual
operating conditions. Now, let's get
into the pitch. The biggest mistake that
I see operators making when they are
pitching consignment is that they're
pitching the wrong thing. They walk up
to a guy with a Ferrari or a Lamborghini
in some random parking lot and ask them,
"Hey, let me rent this out and we'll
split the revenue." What an owner hears
when someone says that is, "Oh yeah,
just let me let this random person I've
never met make money off of my $300,000
car. And the conversation is over before
it even started. That's not the pitch.
That's a sales attempt from someone who
doesn't understand the customer. To run
this pitch correctly, you have to
understand what wealthy car owners
actually want. And it's not going to be
what you think. They don't want the
extra income. A person who owns a
$300,000 Ferrari is not sitting up at
night wondering how they can squeeze an
extra couple of thousand dollars a month
out of the car. Of course, the income
matters, but it is not the lead
motivator. What they actually want is
three things. The first thing is they
want the car to be driven. Exotic cars
just sitting in garages actually creates
severe problems for the cars. Fluids
degrade, seals dry out, batteries die,
it creates flat spots on the tires. The
longer the car sits, the more expensive
it actually becomes to maintain. Most
exotic car owners that I talk to drive
less than 2,000 miles a year cars. And
the car is depreciating whether it's
sitting or not. And it's quietly costing
them money in maintenance even when
they're not touching the car. The second
thing is they want depreciation that
actually makes sense. A new Lamborghini
typically loses around 30% of its
original purchase value when it's brand
new in the first year and continues to
depreciate from then on. If the car is
just sitting, that depreciation is a
pure loss. If the car is generating
income while it depreciates, suddenly
the math changes. Now, at least some of
the depreciation is offset by cash flow.
And also, that depreciation now becomes

That sentence, if you say it enough, will get repeated at the right dinner table conversation eventually. You don't need to find a hundred owners. You need to find three or four solid ones in your first year. That's it. Here is a real-world example. I had a customer who rented a car for me that I actually brokered through another rental company. I met the customer, he wanted to rent a specific car for an event. It was a McLaren. So, he rented the car and he just so happened to own an AMG GT Coupe of his own. Well, turns out he already was brokering this car out with other companies, but he did not trust the other companies and he was barely getting any activities on the car. As soon as we brokered him the car, we had the conversation cuz we saw his car right there parked at the event location. Hey, have you ever considered renting out this AMG GT just like you're renting this McLaren from us? He said, "Yeah, actually I've already brokered it to other companies, but they seem a little bit shady, not getting a lot of business, and they just don't seem that trustworthy." What we did is we showed them what our fleet looked like. We showed them the numbers that these cars were producing for the car owners as well as the tax benefits. He said, "Okay, cool. I'm going to give you guys this AMG GT to rent." Well, as soon as we listed the car for rent, he was so hung up on the numbers we showed him on other vehicles, he ended up trading it in for a Corvette C8. He brought that into the fleet, and the first month that car produced over $4,000 a month gross. His payment on the car was just over 15 or $1,600. Just a week later, he calls me up and he goes, "Hey, Etienne, I'm on my way down to you. I just bought a Lamborghini Huracan Coupe." As soon as we got that car, it was doing about $10,000 a month gross right off the bat. What ended up happening was he went on to buy an Aston Martin Vantage, a BMW i8, and he brought in other investors because we were paying him a royalty that brought us four extra vehicles in the fleet. He was getting 60% of the revenue, we were taking 40%, and that is one of the best deals that we ever closed. Not to mention, he brought a lot of customers and was even renting some of the cars from the fleet as well. Now, we need to talk about the contract terms that protects [music] both parties. Pitching the deal is one thing, but structuring it is another. A bad consignment contract will eat you alive. A good one is the foundation of a scalable fleet. Here is what mine includes at a high level. Also, this is not legal advice, so get a lawyer, but this is the framework. You want to talk about the term length. The term length in my personal contract is there's no obligation. I do not want any vehicle owner to feel trapped. However, I do recommend that they leave the car with us for at least one quarter because usually within a quarter you will see at least one good month. The next thing is you clearly want to outline the revenue split. The standard market is somewhere between 60/40 and 70/30 split, usually in the owner's favor. I like to start at 50/50, especially depending on the vehicle. If an owner brings me multiple vehicles or really specialty vehicle, I will go to 60/40. You also want to outline the maintenance responsibility. This needs to be spelled out in detail. Who pays for the routine maintenance, how damage should be handled when it's on rental versus off rental, especially if they did the damage or a team member did the damage. And then, you want to talk about insurance. This is the section that a lawyer should write. Making sure that the vehicle is covered both off and on trip have to be clearly defined and how that's done. Remember, an owner's personal policy will not cover commercial use, so you need to make sure that the vehicle is covered properly both off and on trip. If you let the renter take a car out on a rental and all it has is an owner's personal policy on it, you're potentially one accident away from a lawsuit that's going to end you and your business. Another thing you need to line out in the contract is use restrictions. What are the mileage caps per day per rental? What are the mileage allotments for marketing and things that such as maintenance and delivery? What are the geographic restrictions, speed and tracking provisions, whatever protects the asset. You also need to have a termination clause in there. Both sides need a clean exit in the contract. Ours is we need at least 48 hours written notice to terminate the contract from either party. You also want to be clear about performance reporting. The owner should get a monthly statement with the utilization, the revenue that it brought in, any relevant expenses, the split, and mileage reporting. Transparency is going to build trust, and that trust is going to get you your next consignment deal. This contract is what's going to separate a hobby [snorts] from a real business. Most people who try consignment and fail, they fail at this part. They had the pitch, they just didn't have the structure. So, that's the consignment playbook. Understand what wealthy owners actually want, open with their pain point and not your offer, walk them through the three scenario math, source from car meets, detailing shops, Instagram, existing customers, and your existing network. Lock it down with a contract that's been reviewed by a lawyer. Done correctly, this is how you scale a rental fleet from one, two cars to 10 plus cars very, very fast and without putting your own capital at risk. But, [music] done incorrectly, you'll lose deals, lose owners, and lose your reputation in your local [music] market. There is no in between. If you're running a fleet right now and you want to scale, or you're just getting started, click the first link in the description and book a strategy call. We'll map out your specific market, your starter vehicles, and your first 60-day scale plan. I only take a limited number of these calls, and I keep my student circle small because this is a true one-on-one mentorship. Thanks again for watching. Don't forget to like, subscribe, [music] and comment, and we'll see you in the next video.

Building a car rental business in Baltimore starts with a single vehicle. Learn how Alex Afosu scaled his fleet to over 50 cars.

Alex Auto shares his journey from a one-car startup to running the top car rental business in his local market. He explains his focus on providing reliable transportation for gig workers and the operational consistency required to manage a fleet of this size over four years.

This breakdown covers the essential steps of fleet management and how to scale your operations effectively. If you want to build a sustainable car rental business, follow along for more insights on managing your vehicles and maintaining steady growth.

metadata.shortDescription:
Start & Scale A Luxury Rental Business:  https://luxcarrent-sler8qjk.manus.space/#contact 

In this full breakdown, I'm walking you through my journey from flipping salvage title cars on Copart to building a full-fledged exotic car rental business with three locations across major cities. It wasn't easy — I learned everything the hard way, from buying my first $1,800 Altima with a $29 tool set to getting crushed by Turo's 25-30% cut once I started scaling. This is how I pivoted out of the platform model and built my own brand with my own insurance, my own CRM, and my own clientele.

I Cover: 
✅ How I got started — buying salvage cars on Copart, teaching myself repairs with no YouTube tutorials 
✅ Why mentorship changed everything — the dealer who took me under his wing 
✅ Scaling from 2 cars to 50+ economy cars on Turo before I saw the trap 
✅ The 25-30% cut problem — why I Peace'd out of Turo and built my own company 
✅ Partnering with insurance companies that cover all 50 states (no $200K limit like Turo) 
✅ Building the operational stack — CRM, invoicing, reimbursement systems, everything 
✅ Why market research matters — the BMW that flopped because I bought wrong 
✅ The exotic and luxury pivot — Maybachs, Cadillacs, and chauffeur services 
✅ Financial freedom and quality of life — why this beats any desk job

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Car Rental Fleet
metadata.author: Money Prism
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it really take to own a car rental fleet, and how does it make money? In this video, we break down the economics of the car rental business: how fleets are bought and financed, why depreciation is the biggest cost, what utilization really means, and why a rental company often looks like a used car lot that gets paid to wait.

Car rental looks simple. Buy cars, rent them out, collect cash. But every vehicle loses value every single day, insurance and maintenance never stop, and an idle car earns nothing. We look at how companies like Hertz, Avis, and Enterprise manage fleet size, buy-back programs, airport fees, pricing, and resale timing, and why one bad stretch in the used car market can push a giant rental company toward bankruptcy.

In this video you will learn:

How a car rental fleet makes money
Why depreciation is the single biggest expense
What utilization is and why every idle day hurts
How rental companies finance thousands of vehicles
How airport fees, insurance, and maintenance cut into profit
Why fleet resale timing can make or break the business
How Hertz, Avis, and Enterprise compete
Whether owning a car rental fleet is actually a good business

If you enjoy business breakdowns and “how does this actually make money” videos, subscribe for more.

👍 Like the video if you learned something new
💬 Comment: would you want to own a car rental fleet?
🔔 Subscribe and turn on notifications for new videos every week

Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not financial or investment advice.

Hashtags:
#CarRental #Hertz #Avis #Enterprise #BusinessModel #Finance #Investing #Economics #BusinessBreakdown #HowItWorks
