segments.text: Okay, so you want to own a car rental
fleet. You can see it perfectly. 100
keys on a 100 hooks, a lot full of clean
silver sedans, travelers handing over
credit cards at 8 in the morning, and a
business so simple a child could run it.
Buy the car, rent the car, repeat, the
car is the machine. The machine prints
money, and at the end of the year, you
sell the machine for most of what you
paid for it. Of every business a normal
person can actually buy into, this is
the one that looks most like a vending
machine. Here's what that picture leaves
out. The car is not your product. The
car is your inventory, your collateral,
your single largest expense, and your
exit strategy. And it starts dying the
moment it rolls off the dealer lot.
Every day you own it, it is worth less
than it was the day before. There is no
way to stop that. The only question in
this entire business is whether the
money you collect by renting it out runs
faster than the money it quietly loses
while sitting still. Everything else is
decoration. And that means the thing you
think you're selling, you're not selling
at all. Which is why the first thing you
have to understand is that a car rental
fleet isn't really a rental business.
It's a used car lot that figured out how
to get paid to wait. Stay with me
because once you see it that way, every
number in this industry reorganizes
itself around a different center. Most
people's mental model goes like this. A
rental company is a taxi company where
the customer drives. You own cars.
People pay you to use them. The cars
wear out eventually. You replace them.
It's a service business with metal in
it. clean, simple, low margin, but
predictable. That model is wrong in
three separate places, and it's worth
breaking each one before we talk about a
single dollar. First, a rental company
is not one business. It's three
businesses stacked on top of each other,
and they have completely different
economics. It's a financing business
because it buys hundreds of thousands of
cars with borrowed money and must
service that debt whether or not anyone
shows up. It's an insurance business
because it sells protection products and
absorbs damage, theft, and liability.
And it's a wholesale used car business
because at the end of every vehicle's
life, it has to sell the metal into an
auction market it does not control. The
rental counter is the thing that
connects all three. It is not the profit
center, it's the meter. Second, and this
is the reversal that surprises almost
everyone who looks at the filings for
the first time. There have been years
where the big rental companies made more
money from their cars increasing in
value than from renting them. In 2022,
Avis Budget Group reported record
revenue of roughly 12 billion and about
$3.7 billion of adjusted EBA in the
Americas alone. Adjusted EBA quickly is
profit before interest, taxes, and the
accounting wear and tear on the cars. A
rough measure of cash the operation
throws off. And a serious slice of that
record year came from something nobody
at the counter did. The used cars Avis
already owned were suddenly worth far
more than the company had written them
down to. The fleet appreciated. Fleets
are not supposed to appreciate. Third,
the customer is not the person handing
you the credit card. In the largest and
most profitable slice of the American
rental market, the person choosing the
company, setting the price, and paying
the bill is somebody else entirely.
We'll get there. So, let's start at the
beginning with the cost of merely being
allowed to do this because this is a
business where the money goes out long
before a single car turns a wheel. You
can't just buy 10 cars and hang a sign.
At an airport, and airports are where
the money is, you don't rent space. You
win a concession. A concession is a
contract granting you the exclusive or
semi-exclusive right to operate at that
airport, and you win it by bidding. And
the bid is not a flat rent check. It's
typically a percentage of your gross
revenue, commonly somewhere in the 10 to
12% range plus something called a
minimum annual guarantee or magi.fleat.
A mag is the floor payment you owe the
airport whether or not you rent a single
car. If your percentage share for the
year comes out below the floor, you pay
the floor anyway. So, in a bad year,
you're not just losing money on empty
cars, you're writing a check to an
airport authority for the privilege of
having failed there. Airports know
exactly how valuable car rentals are. By
the way, the industry's own trade data
suggests rental car concessions can
account for something close to 40% of an
airport's non-airine revenue. You are
not a tenant. You are a revenue line
item in somebody else's budget. Then
there's the capital. A single midsize
sedan costs somewhere around 28 to
$35,000 new. And a serious airport
operation needs hundreds of them, often
thousands. Nobody pays cash. You use
fleet financing. historically something
called floor plan financing where a
lender pays the dealer for the car and
you owe the lender with the car itself
pledged as collateral or you securitize.
You bundle thousands of vehicles and
their rental cash flows into bonds and
sell those bonds to investors. That's an
assetback security and it's how the
giants fund the fleet. An asset back
security is just a way of turning a
parking lot full of cars into a tradable
investment product. Which brings us to
the least romantic sentence in this
entire script. The bank owns your cars.
You are a caretaker with a profit and
loss statement. When Herz missed roughly
$400 million of payments on exactly this
kind of facility in late April 2020, the
machinery of ownership revealed itself
instantly. More on that in a minute.
First, which fleet are we even talking
about? Because car rental is at least
five different businesses wearing the
same uniform. Airport rentals are the
glamorous ones. high daily rates, high
costs, brutal seasonality, corporate
travel accounts, and customers who care
about speed above everything else. Which
is why the loyalty programs, the skip
the counter apps, and the preferred lots
exist. The off airport neighborhood
branch is a different animal. Cheaper
real estate, local customers, insurance
replacement work, repair shop drop offs,
people whose own car is in the body
shop. Then there's the insurance
replacement business specifically, which
is enormous and invisible to the public.
Then exotic and luxury rental, a
completely different economic model
where utilization is low, deposits are
high, and the asset sometimes doesn't
depreciate. And now there's the platform
model where a company owns software
instead of cars and let strangers rent
out their own vehicles. Here's the
reversal hiding in that list. The most
profitable, most durable, least famous
segment of the American rental business
is the one where the customer doesn't
choose you, doesn't compare you, doesn't
review you, and often doesn't even pay
you. We'll come back to that because it
explains the single most important
strategic decision anyone has ever made
in this industry. Now, the costs nobody
puts in the listing. You buy the cars,
but you don't own a business yet. You
need a lot. And not just any lot, but
one near where customers are with a
washbay, a fueling position, a lighting
setup, a fence, a key cabinet, and
enough space to park a portion of your
fleet that will be idle on any given
day. You need shuttle buses if you're at
an airport. And shuttle buses are
spectacularly expensive per passenger.
You need cleaning staff because every
car has to be turned around between
rentals, vacuumed, washed, fueled,
inspected, and it has to happen in
minutes, not hours, on a holiday
weekend. You need software that does
yield management, which is the airline
trick of changing your price based on
how many cars are left and how soon they
go out. You need damage inspection
because the difference between what a
customer did to a car and what you can
prove a customer did to a car is worth
hundreds of thousands of dollars a year.
And here's the thing that eats people
alive. Every one of those costs scales
with the car, but the car's value falls
whether or not it's used. A car parked
at the back of your lot waiting for a
customer is a car losing roughly $10 to
$15 a day in value plus insurance plus
registration plus its share of the rent
on the asphalt it's sitting on. Idle
inventory in this business doesn't just
fail to earn. It actively bills you. So
how do you fight back? You sell more
things. The revenue model is where this
industry stops looking like a car
business and starts looking like an
airport terminal newsstand. Yes, there's
the base daily rate, what everyone
thinks of as the price. But the daily
rate is often the least profitable line
on the entire contract. The real money
sits in the extras. The loss damage
waiver, the fuel service option, the
additional driver fee, the young driver
search charge, the toll transponder, the
child seat, the GPS unit, the one-way
drop fee, the late return fee, the
cleaning fee if you smoke in it. The
loss damage waiver deserves a full stop
because it's the most misunderstood
product in the industry. It's not
insurance. Legally, it's a waiver of
your responsibility for damage to the
vehicle sold by the rental company. And
it typically costs $15 to $30 a day on
top of a rate that might be 50 or 60.
Think about the ratio. That's a product
priced at half the cost of the actual
rental with a claims experience that
most customers never touch. It is by
margin one of the best businesses in
travel. And when you're standing at a
counter at 11 at night, exhausted in an
unfamiliar city, and someone asks
whether you want to be responsible for a
$30,000 car, that's not a sales pitch.
That's a negotiation with your own
anxiety. The rental company knows
precisely what it's selling you, and it
isn't protection. It's peace of mind
priced at the moment you're least able
to think clearly. Then there's a revenue
stream that isn't a fee at all, and it's
bigger than any of them, the resale.
Which brings us to the central paradox.
The thing this entire industry is built
around and almost never says out loud.
You would assume the customer is the
source of the profit. The customer pays,
therefore the customer is the profit.
That's how every normal business works.
A restaurant's profit comes from diners.
A gym's profit comes from members. The
transaction is the business. In a rental
fleet, the transaction is not the
business. The transaction is the
financing. Write that again. Your rental
revenue has to cover depreciation,
interest, staff, insurance, maintenance,
the concession fee, and the lot. And
after all of that, whatever is left is
thin, volatile, and often negative. What
actually determines whether you get rich
or get wiped out are two numbers that
have nothing to do with your customers.
What you paid for the car on the day you
bought it, and what it's worth on the
day you sell it. The customer is
standing in the middle of those two
numbers, paying your carrying costs
while you wait. That's the paradox, and
it gets stranger. Depreciation is not a
fact. It's an estimate, an assumption
management chooses about what the car
will be worth in 18 or 24 months, spread
across each month you own it. The
industry tracks this obsessively as
depreciation per unit, or DPU, how many
dollars each car in the fleet loses per
month. In late 2024, Hertz was reporting
gross depreciation per unit of about
$347 a month with a target of getting
below 300. $350 a month on a car that
might rent for $1,500 a month at 80%
utilization. The depreciation is not a
line item in this business. It's the
atmosphere. Now, put those two facts
together and you arrive at something
genuinely unsettling. The largest cost
in the business is a guess. The guess is
made by the people reporting the profit
and the thing being guessed at trades
daily in an auction market nobody
controls. The Mannheim Used Vehicle
Value Index, the industry's wholesale
price thermometer, built from millions
of auction transactions, can move 20% in
a year when it moves billions of dollars
of book value move with it. And it all
lands in the same earnings report as the
rental revenue, indistinguishable to a
casual reader. That is why this business
can be full and still bleed. A packed
lot in July tells you nothing. The
fleet's value on the day you sell it
tells you everything. You can run the
best counter in the country, greet every
customer by name, never lose a car,
never have a complaint, and still lose
$40 million because a manufacturer cut
prices in March. And if you don't
believe that, let me introduce you to
the company that learned it the hardest
way available. Herz, then one of the two
dominant names on Earth, roughly a
century old, the company that invented
the airport rental counter as a mass
market idea, filed for Chapter 11
bankruptcy protection on the 22nd of
May, 2020. Chapter 11 is a legal shelter
where a company keeps operating while it
renegotiates its debts, protected from
creditors. It walked in with about a
billion dollars of cash in hand and
something close to $19 billion of debt
on its books. 19 billion for a company
whose physical assets are cars that lose
value every day. Here's the timeline,
and here's the part people get wrong.
The pandemic is usually blamed. It
didn't help. But look at the actual
order of events. In late April 2020,
Herz failed to make roughly $400 million
of payments on its fleet financing
facilities. That happened before demand
collapsed entirely. And it happened
because the company was structured with
almost no cushion. It had borrowed
against cars. And cars are excellent
collateral right up until the moment
nobody wants to buy them. That's the
structural lesson. Leverage against a
depreciating asset feels safe because
the asset is right there, visible,
tangible, insured. But the asset's value
is set by a market. And in March and
April of 2020, that market briefly
stopped being a market at all. Dealers
closed. Auctions went online only.
Wholesale prices whipssawed violently.
Herz had agreed to sell huge numbers of
vehicles at prices set before anyone
knew what was happening. and the timing
of those sales was catastrophic. It was
a company that had been brilliant at
renting cars and had been unable to stop
itself from becoming a leveraged bet on
used car prices. Revenue was never the
problem. The balance sheet was the
problem. And here's the detail that
should genuinely rattle you about this
industry. Herz emerged from bankruptcy,
cut over $5 billion of debt in the
reorganization, and then in December
2022 agreed to pay $168 million to
settle claims from 3 64 customers whose
rentals had been reported to police as
stolen, some of whom were arrested at
gunpoint in front of their families. The
approximate cause was paperwork and
process, not cars, not demand, not
pricing $364,
$460,000 each on average. A business
that can absorb $168 million of goodwill
damage from clerical failure is a
business with an enormous amount of
operating leverage. Meaning small
process failures become enormous
financial events. In most industries, a
paperwork mistake is a paperwork
mistake. Here it's a lawsuit with a
police report attached. So Herz survived
the pandemic. Surely having learned that
leverage against depreciating metal is
dangerous, it became conservative. It
did the opposite. And this is the second
case study. and honestly the better one
because it involves smart people with
excellent information making a bet that
failed in a way nobody forecast. In
October 2021, Herz announced it would
order a 100,000 Teslas. A deal reported
at around $4.2 billion and at the time
the largest single purchase of electric
vehicles ever made by anyone. It was a
strategy statement, a marketing event
and a genuine bet all at once. Electric
cars, the pitch went, cost less than a
fuel and less to maintain. They'd
attract a new kind of customer, and this
was the crucial assumption. They'd hold
their value. Tesla was the hottest brand
in the world. Their resale prices had
been extraordinary for years. You can
probably see the flaw. The manufacturer
who sold you the fleet controls the
price of the product your fleet competes
against. Tesla spent 2023 and 2024
cutting new car prices repeatedly and
aggressively. Every cut made a new Tesla
cheaper, which meant every used Tesla
became worth less, including the tens of
thousands sitting on Hertz lots. By
early 2024, Hertz was disclosing roughly
a half billion dollars of write downs
and losses connected to its EV fleet.
And by the end of 2024, it reported a
fullear net loss of about $2.9 billion.
Its chief executive, Steven Sher,
departed in March 2024. By year end, the
fleet was about 7% smaller than it had
been at the start of the year. Fewer
cars because fewer cars was the only
honest answer. And note what happened to
the assumptions. Electric vehicles did
cost less to fuel. They did cost less to

metadata.title: Black Car vs. Uber: The REAL Difference Between Luxury Transportation & Rideshare
metadata.author: Luxury Transportation Academy / Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Ever wonder why some clients will NEVER book a rideshare? 🚘

In this episode of The Luxury Transportation Podcast, host Durrell Willis and Dr. Morris Parker (CEO of TCW Limo & founder of the Luxury Transportation Academy) break down the real difference between rideshare/taxi services and true luxury black car transportation — and why that difference translates directly into trust, retention, and revenue.

From the origins of personal chauffeur service for the elite, to today's rideshare landscape, this conversation unpacks what high-net-worth clients actually expect — and why "good enough" doesn't cut it in this industry.

🎙️ In this episode, we cover:
✅ Why small changes in value & process drive year-over-year growth
✅ The hidden cost of platforms like Uber Black/Business/Corporate (10-20% revenue cut)
✅ Why building direct client & corporate account relationships beats relying on rideshare platforms
✅ The origin story of luxury transportation — from elite personal drivers to modern black car service
✅ Rideshare horror stories vs. the professionalism of a vetted, trained chauffeur
✅ Why discretion, safety, and personalized service are what clients are really paying for
✅ How giving clients "time back" is the true value proposition of luxury transportation

Whether you're new to the industry (like "Joe" buying his first vehicle) or a seasoned operator with a growing fleet (like "Bob" navigating industry changes), this episode lays the groundwork for building a business rooted in trust and long-term client relationships.

📌 Want to build a business people trust enough to keep coming back to? Learn more about the Luxury Transportation Academy (LTA) and the mentorship available to help you grow.

👉 Subscribe for new episodes of The Luxury Transportation Podcast every week!

#LuxuryTransportation #BlackCarService #UberBlack #ChauffeurLife #RideshareVsLuxury #LimoBusiness #EntrepreneurPodcast #LTAAcademy #GroundTransportation #ClientTrust

segments.text: What's up, Mavericks?
Does your business rely on vehicles for delivering goods,
transporting clients, or driving to job sites?
If so, you already know the importance of reliable
commercial auto insurance to keep your business moving forward.
But sifting through countless insurance options
feels like getting stuck in traffic during rush hour.
That's why we've done the heavy lifting for you.
Today, we're counting down the top 5 commercial auto insurance
providers to help you find the right coverage for your business.
Make sure to stick around until the end to see our top pick. Coming in at number five is Nationwide.
We've all heard the jingle, and Nationwide is
on your side even if you manage a large fleet of commercial vehicles.
Nationwide is a provider that lives up to its name
by offering extensive coverage across more than 40 states.
If you're managing a fleet, Nationwide's specialized policies are designed with
you in mind, providing customizable commercial auto insurance options,
including liability, collision, and comprehensive coverage.
Nationwide also offers options if you borrow or
rent cars or if your employees use personal vehicles for work.
Nationwide's fleet management tools and
risk assessment services help keep your operations running smoothly.
As with other providers on this list,
Nationwide requires you to get a custom quote for your coverage.
You can do this by calling Nationwide's toll free number,
working with an agent, or requesting one online through the Nationwide website.
Next on our list is another heavy hitter.
Progressive Commercial Insurance is a provider that's renowned for
its flexibility and extensive coverage options.
Progressive has tailored policies to fit your needs including truck insurance,
motor cargo, and trailer interchange policies.
Progressive offers a range of coverages including liability, physical damage,
and uninsured motorist protection.
Twenty four seven claim service and a network of repair shops ensure that
you're back on the road quickly after an incident.
Progressive does offer some transparency by providing average and median prices
for different policies, but you still need a personalized quote.
You can easily get a quote and start coverage directly through Progressive's website.
If you want to learn more about Progressive or any of the other providers on our list,
make sure to check out our full reviews linked down in the description below.
NEXT Insurance is our number three pick for its bundled discounts.
Although NEXT Insurance doesn't underwrite commercial auto insurance directly,
it partners with Progressive, another one of our top picks.
So why choose NEXT instead of working directly with Progressive?
NEXT offers bundled discounts, allowing you to combine commercial auto insurance
with other policies like general liability and workers' compensation.
With two or more policies, you can save 10% on NEXT'S already competitive pricing.
NEXT user friendly online platform provides instant quotes and streamlined
policy management, making it easy to get the coverage you need without paperwork.
If you want competitive pricing without sacrificing quality,
our runner-up, BiBERK, has you covered.
This Berkshire Hathaway company offers direct to
business insurance solutions that help you save money.
BiBERK provides commercial auto insurance policies with liability, collision,
and comprehensive coverage, optional add ons like rental reimbursement and roadside
assistance, and and roadside assistance are also available.
BiBERK covers nearly any type of vehicle from pickup trucks and
company cars to larger flatbed trucks or emergency vehicles.
You'll need a personalized quote to see your monthly cost,
but BiBERK claims customers save up to 20% by cutting out the middleman.
BiBERK's online platform allows for quick quotes and easy policy management,
making the entire process hassle free.
And topping our list is our number one pick,
The Hartford, provider with over 200 years of experience in protecting businesses.
The Hartford stands out for its comprehensive coverage options,
exceptional customer service, and strong financial stability.
The Hartford offers coverage for any situation including the basics like liability and physical
damage, to more specialized coverage like drive other car endorsements, also known as CA 99 10.
You can get a quote online and with twenty four seven claims assistance and personalized service.
The Hartford helps keep your business vehicles well protected and on the road.
To learn more or get started with a free quote, visit merchantmaverick.com/thehartford.
And that covers our countdown of the five best commercial auto insurance providers.
Whether you're looking for nationwide coverage, fleet management solutions, competitive pricing,
or comprehensive protection, there's an option tailored to your business needs.
If you're still weighing your options, be sure to check out our full list of the best commercial
auto insurance and our in-depth reviews, all linked down in the description below.
Thanks for watching Mavericks.
Stay safe out there and we'll see you in the next video!

metadata.title: The B2B Rental Strategy Behind His 277-Vehicle Fleet
metadata.author: FleetPilot
metadata.shortDescription:
What does it take to keep 277 rental vehicles moving year-round—without depending entirely on Turo?

In this episode of The Fleet Operator Podcast, James sits down with Steve Ludwig, founder of Select Auto Rentals, to unpack the B2B rental strategy behind his 277-vehicle fleet of passenger vans, Suburbans, Yukons and Escalades.

Steve’s rental business started with three Escalades after a friend showed him what he was earning from his fleet. Two vehicles became 20, 20 became 200, and the operation eventually grew to 277 vehicles in the St. Louis market.

But the real breakthrough wasn’t simply adding more cars. It was shifting away from seasonal consumer rentals and building recurring relationships with businesses, schools, churches, transportation companies, contractors, dealerships and event operators that need vehicles throughout the year.

Steve explains why he sold a Ferrari 488 to buy passenger vans, how a $25,000 van can outperform a $500,000 Airbnb, and why B2B customers can produce more consistent revenue with less wear, lower acquisition costs and greater accountability when damage occurs.

In this episode, we cover:

• How three Escalades eventually became a 277-vehicle rental fleet  
• Why Steve shifted from Airbnb properties into rental vehicles  
• The B2B strategy that keeps his fleet moving year-round  
• Why passenger vans have become the foundation of his business  
• How he works with churches, schools, contractors and transportation companies  
• How his fleet supported major events requiring as many as 80 vehicles  
• Why he sold exotic cars to invest in income-producing vans  
• The economics behind his $1,000 game-day shuttle package  
• Why recurring business relationships can outperform consumer advertising  
• How insurance expertise became a competitive advantage  
• The risks of renting vehicles to rideshare and gig-economy drivers  
• Why fleet operators must track net profit—not just gross revenue  
• How Steve evaluates vehicles without becoming emotionally attached  
• The systems, staffing and operating rules required to manage hundreds of vehicles  
• How outside investors can purchase vehicles and have Select Auto Rentals operate them  
• Why more vehicles do not automatically mean more profit  

Steve also shares an important warning for operators chasing impressive revenue numbers: the gross may look great, but the real business is determined by depreciation, maintenance, labor, downtime, risk and what you actually take home.

Learn more about Select Auto Rentals and Steve’s vehicle investment program:  
https://selectautorentals.com

Put your rental fleet’s financials and operations on autopilot with FleetPilot:  
https://getfleetpilot.com

Subscribe for more conversations with independent fleet operators building profitable rental businesses across Turo, direct bookings, B2B rentals and other channels.

https://www.youtube.com/@GetFleetPilot

#CarRentalBusiness #FleetManagement #TuroHost

So we only have a car, you know, out of 300 cars, we have three or four come back in a day, maybe five. I think the most we've had come back in like a day is like six, which is like that's kind of a lot. Now there's downsides to it. There's harder customers, there's repossessions. I mean, there's things like that. But once you have the right systems put in place, it's much easier to manage. Now, the third thing you want to think about when scaling is financing. How do I actually get financing for these cars? A lot of people like this play where they go to the dealership, buy a car, maybe they buy two cars. Then they go to they go to another dealership within a 7-day period cuz that's when they report it to the credit unions or the other banks or something like that. I think that's the timeframe. I could be wrong. And they buy another car, and then they go to another dealership and repeat, and they buy like 10 cars or 15 cars a week, and that is insane. And my biggest my my problem with it isn't the concept. The concept is fine. Like, if you decide to go out and buy 20 cars in a week, um that's not the problem. But, the problem is the fact that people are trying to buy them so quick that they're not doing any research on the kind of cars that they're buying. And so, they're getting bad loans, bad terms, wrong cars that they're buying, wrong prices. They're just not caring. They're saying, "Hey, kind of like in the beginning of the video I mentioned, it's not just about adding cars, it's about adding them the right way and scaling them the right way." And so, people just say, "Yeah, like let me just buy as many cars as I can because people are putting this concept out there of just add cars, just buy cars, just add your buy cars quick as more cars you have, the more profitable you are, which is completely wrong. All right. So, the fourth and final thing I want to talk about is how you rent your car out. Now, a lot of people think there's one way to rent your car out Turo. And a lot of people are going to preach like, "Oh, you should rent your car on Turo. You should rent your car on Turo." I believe in that, too. I believe that for the first couple months of renting cars out, you should use Turo. True. But, once you start doing direct rentals, like somebody books through your website, somebody comes to you to rent the car, you make significantly more money. We made that transition about a year ago, last April. Not because we wanted to. We had started to at the time. We had like 30%, 20% of our rentals off of the platform, but we got kicked off of Turo, and so kind of forced us to make the transition. Best thing ever. People always say, "Well, they always try to give me ideas like, can't you do this and get back on Turo or do that?" And I'm like, "I don't want to." Like, "Don't you don't want to get back on Turo?" I'm like, "No. I'm making two times the amount that I would have if I was on Turo. Why would I want to go back to that? Like, isn't the concept to make more money here, not less?" And like, the systems that they have aren't better than the systems that I have. I have It's easier for me to manage my fleet now than if I were there. So, like, why would I want that? A lot of people want to build their business and scale it. Some people don't. Some people have it as a side hustle, two or three cars. I'm going to run it side hustle. I have a main job. That's fine. Which is that's completely fine. If you're doing something like that, stay on Turo. Don't transition cuz there's a lot of things you have to set up. But, if you do decide to make the transition, that's probably the best decision anyone can make. Like, for me, it's best decision. Obviously, it wasn't really my decision, but it's the best thing that had happened to us ever. And when you're renting directly to customers, there's tons of ways you can do it. I mean, you can you can do right your rentals, which is what we do, Uber and Lyft drivers, long-term rentals. You can do like short-term travelers or local. You can do mechanic shop work, which is when cars are in a mechanic shop. And I guess you can kind of fuse a lot of these together. And the best resource that we found for this is actually something that we helped build, and it's something called Ifly. It's a software built for uh fleet operators to do direct rentals. And it literally has everything. If you want to make the transition, or if you're already doing direct rentals, we've used HQ, we've used Wheelbase, we've used everything. And problems were systems weren't good, or it's too expensive, didn't have what we needed. But we built it the way an operator would see it. And we built it the exact way that we'd want it. Has booking, payment collection process, insurance verification, you can sell insurance through it. You can do background checks, you can text directly to the customer, email directly to them. So like full email system and communication system built out, comm system. Has all of our tracking information built in, website builder, marketing system. Like it literally has everything that we would need. Claims management, toll management. Like before we had this, we had seven, I think, or eight different softwares we'd used. We had to go back and forth to all these different ones. Now it's one. Now instead of my team having to like figure out how to go between all these different softwares, figure out how to use them, and like the training super complex, it's like, okay, one software, here's how you use it. Super simple. So whether you're running yourself or other people are running it, like best solution ever. Honestly, the builders were able to give it away for like 99 bucks a month, which is the cheapest on the market. So it's best solution, cheapest on the market, what could go wrong? 14-day free trial, I think it's set up right now. Honestly, just check it out. It's insane. This is something that we're going to use fully for our fleet, and I'd highly recommend it for yours. Like it's it's cool, very cool. Well, thanks for watching the video. I hope this helped you a little bit. I hope you don't make a lot of the mistakes that tons of people talk about, and I'll see you in the next video. Peace.

metadata.title: How I Scaled My Turo Fleet to 15 Cars (The Remote CEO Blueprint)
metadata.author: Brandon Ascari
metadata.shortDescription:
I went from one Honda Civic to a 15-car fleet while owning a production company and eventually traveling to Japan with my wife and our two young kids. In this video, I break down the exact scaling story I went through to build a remote Turo business that runs without me. 

JOIN THE FLEET FREEDOM WAITLIST: https://fleetfreedom.kit.com/673cfce1a0 
(We go live when we hit 1,000 subscribers!) 

What we cover in this video: 

The "Value Cliff" car buying strategy. 

How I used a 50/50 investor split to scale faster. 

Managing the "Murder Mini-Van" and total loss claims. 

My remote operations stack for managing cars from 7,000 miles away. 

#turorial #PassiveIncome #FleetMastermind #RemoteCEO #SideHustle #BusinessScaling #FinancialFreedom

Discover how CEO Mo scaled from Turo to a 250+ car fleet in Detroit — all through private rentals. In this episode of Elevate Car Rentals, we dive into the strategies, struggles, and wins of building a car rental empire, covering everything from insurance headaches to repossessions, claims, reinvestment, and growth tactics. Mo also shares insights on the future of rentals, autonomous vehicles, and how to scale fast in a high-risk, high-reward industry. If you’re thinking about starting a car rental business or figuring out what to do after your first car, this is the story I wish I’d heard when I was getting started.

metadata.title: 🔍 Turo Peer-to-Peer Car Sharing Graves Amendment Liability | Case No. 24-0266 | FL Appellate
metadata.author: Florida Trust, Real Estate, Probate, & Foreclosure
metadata.shortDescription:
Sheller v. Turo, Inc. | Case No. 24-0266 | Florida District Court of Appeal

Attorney Paul Eisolini argues on behalf of appellant Sheller, who was injured in a 2020 motor vehicle accident involving a car shared through Turo's peer-to-peer platform. The trial court granted summary judgment for Turo and the car owner/sharer (Conduri) under the Graves Amendment, which exempts vehicle rental companies from vicarious liability. Appellant argues the Graves Amendment does not apply to peer-to-peer car sharing arrangements and that the Florida legislature's 2022 statute explicitly addressed this issue.

Key issues addressed:
• Graves Amendment (49 U.S.C. §30106) — federal law exempting vehicle rental companies from vicarious liability and its applicability to peer-to-peer sharing platforms
• Whether Turo and individual car sharers are "engaged in the trade or business of renting or leasing motor vehicles" under the Graves Amendment
• Florida 2022 statute on peer-to-peer vehicle sharing and its relationship to the Graves Amendment
• Vicarious liability of car owner (Conduri) who listed vehicle on Turo for commercial gain
• Summary judgment standard — whether material facts were in dispute regarding Turo's business model

🔗 Florida Rules & Legal Resources: www.floridarules.net

#GravesAmendment #Turo #PeerToPeerCarSharing #FloridaAppellate #OralArgument #VehicularLiability #FloridaLaw #AppellateProcedure #PersonalInjury #FloridalAppeal

This was not the first time he's done this. Is there a record on how many other times he's done this? It does not say how many, but he said that this was not his first time. That he had done it before. It didn't say, I don't believe in his deposition transcript, whether or not he was asked how many times he's done it, but he said he's done it before with Turo. So, this is an activity that he does. Like you said, a side hustle. This is something that he would do to add to his income. He doesn't have to just be an IT consultant and take that only income. He can do rental of this car, he could rent his house, he could teach to kids in some virtual capacity. I don't know. He could do anything to to make money. So, there's nothing in the statute to say that you have to be a rental car company in order to do that. Um all the statute requires is Let me ask you one other question number on this. There's one part of the text in in sub paragraph one, the reason I bring it And the owner, I'm just reading, is engaged in the trade or business of renting or leasing motor vehicles, plural. And I don't think there's any record that other than to the extent Mr. owner was being dishonest with Mr. Turo, that it was more than one vehicle. What what how do we know that that the reason that I bring it up is that vehicles plural. >> Okay. So, >> be I mean, that would be a helpful point for your your opponent. I'd like you to address it as well. Okay. So, it he did have two vehicles. He had his wife's vehicle, he had his own vehicle. The the record does say that he only rented out this vehicle. So, that is correct. But, there are multiple vehicles that he has. And I think with the way we have to look at that is that you were engaging in a single act for profit and that could be the business venture. You're engaging in the trade or business of renting the motor vehicles. It's multiple transactions. It doesn't have to necessarily be multiple vehicles. The decision would be that the vehicle renting or leasing motor vehicles could be read to refer to one motor vehicle in multiple transactions. >> Correct. And not necessarily that you have to have a fleet of motor vehicles. And the reason I can make that um interpretation, I think, is because if you turn to the statute and the definition of owner, the definition of owner is listed in three different ways. You have an owner as a person who is a record or beneficial owner, holder of the title, lessor or lesser of the lessee of a motor vehicle. Then you have B, which is um an owner means a person who is entitled to the use and possession of a motor vehicle subject to a security interest in another person. Or C, you have a lessor, lessee, or bailee of a motor vehicle in the trade or business of renting or leasing motor vehicles having the use or possession thereof under lease, bailment, or otherwise. So, the fact that the legislator has defined three different types of owner means that this statute and this amendment couldn't just apply to rental car companies as they are trying to say that it does because that gives you another opportunity to really explain a different situation for because you have a rental car company that owns a fleet of vehicles. And so, that part C would bring the rental car company into play for the Graves Amendment protection under that definition. But, definition A is a record or beneficial owner or title owner. That's Mr. Condori here. And that's why the statute applies in the manner that it does. So, I think the interpretation of trade or business of renting or leasing motor vehicles has to deal with the transaction. How many times he's done the transaction before. This isn't something that is a one-shot deal where um it was suggested on an owner to you know me and and write a little piece of paper one time and and make a payment. That's not what's happening here. This is a transaction. It's clearly a profit-inducing transaction. >> Let me just see if I can simplify your explanation on the definition of owner aspect of owner under the Graves Amendment. What you are saying is that because the Graves Amendment applies to any owner of a vehicle that runs through 664. It doesn't matter if they have multiple vehicles. So I'm not disputing that. I'm just saying that I don't I'm not disputing that. Okay. Correct. And that's what we had here. So we had a record of a rental transaction, a business transaction to a complete stranger. There was no allegations of negligence or criminal wrongdoing. The only reason Mr. Condory was brought into the suit was because he owned the vehicle and he was trying to be brought in for vicarious liability under the dangerous instrumentality uh doctrine. That the trial court properly ruled and went through the analysis step-by-step finding these undisputed facts. So I don't think the fact that it wasn't his livelihood is enough to to send this back in any way. I think the court properly had all the undisputed facts to make a determination that Mr. Condory was not liable under um the dangerous instrumentality doctrine because the Graves Amendment applied to his claim. So wouldn't you love for a jury to decide it be sent back? Um well, there's two counts. So I didn't even get to the second one which was the judge's venture. So as far as this one >> of that kind of count one? On count one, well we would have to determine if there is a if he's vicariously liable. So you go into the regular jury instructions about negligence and then you would go into is he an owner? Is he vicariously liable? There would be a separate jury instruction about whether or not he was the owner. >> So this is this is assuming the Graves Amendment doesn't apply. >> This would be this would be assuming the Graves Amendment doesn't apply. It's not a law. Well, right. Well, then I would say if you're sending it back cuz you're if you determine that it doesn't apply or if you determine that it's your issue, then it goes back to >> accept the notion that the issue of fact was whether it was engaged in business. >> So, then that's what I was going to go into. So, then if you're going to go into specific interrogatory questions where you're going to be asked >> You have to do an interrogatory. An interrogatory. Correct. You have to do special instructions And you have to define straight asking the jury to tell us what the language of the Graves Amendment means. Correct. And whether or not the facts in this particular case apply. And then that's what the court was supposed to do. And that's what the court did here. And so, it's really, you know, would be silly, I think, to go back to the jury to have a jury go into, you know, determine these factual questions because all the facts are flushed out. The court has everything the court needs to determine and the court has properly determined that the Graves Amendment applied when you strictly construe the plain language of the statute. You read the text, you read it step by step, and you apply the analysis, it applied here to absolve him from vicarious liability. And therefore, summary judgment was proper on that count. And now we also have a second count, which um wasn't addressed, but that was also an account. If you agree that the Graves Amendment did apply, which I think, you know, based on the questioning, that's where the court's leaning, the joint venture can't proceed either because you can't be joint venture liability when you are not negligent and you have no basis for negligence. But, I think, you know, that is something that is also important because of um the evidence that was even proffered to try to get out of summary judgment on that count was a contract that was attached based on a printout from the website. So, then Is there any evidence uh um um for count two? Is there any evidence um an agreement or understanding that the parties would share profits and losses? No, there's nothing. There's nothing to indicate that they would share any losses. As far as the profits go, it's you pay, I do cut. Tour Tour determines what the cut is for each transaction, but there is no agreement to bind each other for anything. And in fact, what I was going to say, although I don't think the court could even consider the contract because it was unauthenticated, it was just pulled from the website. But if you look at page 399 of the contract, it specifically says, "This is not a joint venture." There's nothing in this agreement that establishes a joint venture. So, there is no way that the court could have found joint venture liability. Therefore, the court properly granted summary judgment in Condorey and Tour's favor on that count as well. And then we would ask the jury to do what juries do, apply the facts to the law to make a determination on that interrogatory, preliminary interrogatory question. Your Honor brought up an excellent point. I actually had it in my notes that motor vehicles is plural in the statute. And I think that goes back to the original intent of the statute. I I I am just old enough to remember uh before the Graves Amendment and and I'm a defense attorney by trade where a rental car companies would regularly be joined in lawsuits when they someone was driving and committed a negligent act. Um and we saw a public policy reason to correct that, the federal government did, and the state of Florida did as well. And we adopted that to get rid of that. Then, in the case decided by Rosado, Rosado v. Chrysler, uh Florida make clear that also extends to uh long-term leasing companies like Chrysler when you when you do a long-term lease of a vehicle, we're going to apply the Graves Amendment to that as well. Um if you have any more questions for me, otherwise again >> any lemonades in your car? What? I I I I I've got I have You have lemonades or I have I have the Girl Scout cookies. I do have I do have those No, they they're about to those are about to I can answer some questions about that. You better get them while you can because those and the s'more s'mores are short-lived, but I do have Do-si-dos. >> [laughter] >> Thank you. >> Thank you. That being our last case, uh we are adjourned. All rise.

metadata.shortDescription:
🌵❌🔥The rideshare economy changed how people move. Uber, Lyft, and similar platforms made it easier to get from one place to another, but they also created a legal and political question that is getting harder to ignore: when something goes wrong, who is responsible?

That question sits at the center of the debate around the Graves Amendment and rideshare liability, and the two hosts of Cactus Crossfire, @sistoaabeyta  and @ezableser, tackled it directly in Season 2 Episode 6. 

READ THE FULL BLOG HERE: https://www.cactuscrossfire.com/post/uber-the-graves-amendment-and-the-rideshare-liability-fight

WATCH THE FULL CONVERSATION: https://youtu.be/yaIZKjuw0wA

FULL EPISODE ON APPLE PODCASTS: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/cactus-crossfire/id1859717200?i=1000759520261

Whether you have 1 car or 10, this is what you need to know before your next rental goes out.

Today we learn how fleet vehicle depreciation, residual value tracking, mileage accumulation, and tax deduction strategies impact your commercial car operations. Managing a fleet requires understanding how fast your assets lose market value, how high mileage reduces trade-in returns, and how to structure your commercial expenses properly. By taking full advantage of tax provisions like section 179 and accelerated depreciation, commercial vehicle owners can lower annual taxable income while maintaining strong balance sheet equity. Watch the full video, like the video if you found it helpful, and subscribe to the channel for more commercial fleet insights.

segments.text: Welcome back to Camber Hazard, your
primary destination for deep insights
into commercial transport, vehicle
maintenance, and practical fleet
economics. Today, we are breaking down
one of the largest silent expenses in
business operations, fleet vehicle asset
depreciation. When you run a commercial
fleet or operate a business vehicle,
watching money evaporate through vehicle
value loss can feel overwhelming.
Understanding how residual value,
mileage impact, and tax write-offs fit
together is essential for keeping your
business profitable over the long haul.
Vehicle depreciation is simply the
difference between what you paid for a
vehicle initially and what that vehicle
is worth when you eventually sell it.
The moment a new commercial truck or car
leaves the dealership lot, its market
value begins dropping immediately. In
the first year alone, a typical
commercial asset can lose anywhere from
15 to 20% of its original purchase
price. This loss is not just an abstract
line item on paper. It directly affects
your company balance sheet and cash
reserves. Residual value is the
estimated monetary value of a fleet
vehicle at the end of its intended lease
or operating lifetime.
Determining this figure accurately
allows business owners to calculate
total cost of ownership before buying a
single key. If a vehicle retains a
higher percentage of its value after 5
years of service, your actual monthly
operating cost drops significantly.
Fleet managers rely on precise residual
projections to decide whether purchasing
or leasing makes the most economic sense
for their daily routes. Several key
factors drive the residual value of any
commercial vehicle on the market today.
Brand reliability and secondary market
demand play huge roles in deciding what
buyers will pay years down the road.
Vans and light trucks built with proven
engine platforms always hold their value
much better than models prone to
frequent mechanical breakdowns.
Regional climate, fuel efficiency, and
overall industry trends also shift
residual values over multi-year cycles.
The specific options and factory
packages you select when buying a
vehicle also shape its future resale
power.
Choosing neutral paint colors, durable
cargo liners, and standard safety
technology makes a commercial vehicle
far more attractive to secondary buyers.
On the flip side, overly specialized
modifications that cater to only one
specific niche can actually reduce your
pool of potential buyers.
Smart fleet buyers focus on versatile
configurations that appeal to broad
commercial markets when service time
ends.
Mileage remains one of the most
aggressive drivers of vehicle
depreciation across every commercial
sector.
Every single mile added to the odometer
reflects mechanical wear on the engine,
transmission, suspension, and brake
systems. Buyers in the used commercial
market inspect mileage closely because
high figures suggest imminent repair
bills and potential downtime.
Managing how many miles your drivers
accumulate each month is therefore
critical to controlling your vehicle
depreciation curve. Calculating your
true cost per mile is the best way to
monitor how driving distance impacts
your fleet equity. A delivery vehicle
covering 30,000 miles annually will
experience a much faster value drop than
a service van covering 10,000 miles.
Once a commercial asset crosses key
mileage thresholds, such as 100,000
miles, its market value often takes a
sharp downward turn.
Tracking these thresholds helps you
decide when to pull a vehicle off heavy
routes.
Rotating vehicles among different
drivers and routes is an effective
strategy for balancing mileage across
your entire fleet. Assigning
high-distance highway routes to newer
vehicles while using older vans for
short local errands spreads wear more
evenly.
This balance prevents individual units
from accumulating extreme mileage to
quickly while keeping overall fleet
operations running smoothly. Equalizing
odometer readings across your assets
preserves collective balance sheet value
over time. Maintaining comprehensive
service records is your strongest shield
against severe mileage-based
depreciation.
Buyers willingly pay premium prices for
high-mileage commercial vehicles if you
can produce clean, detailed maintenance
logs. Documenting regular oil changes,
fluid flushes, brake replacements, and
inspection reports proves that the
vehicle received continuous professional
care.
Clear records transform a questionable
high-mileage asset into a trustworthy
used vehicle that commands higher resale
offers. While depreciation reduces asset
value, it also provides significant
opportunities for commercial tax
write-offs.
Tax codes allow business owners to
deduct the declining value of their work
vehicles from their annual taxable
income. These deductions lower your
overall tax burden, effectively
recovering a chunk of the money lost to
normal wear and tear.
Knowing how to leverage these tax rules
legally keeps more working capital
inside your commercial bank account. The
Internal Revenue Service established the
Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery
System for deducting business equipment
over time. Under this system, commercial
vehicles are generally classified as
5-year property for tax recovery
purposes. This framework allows business
owners to write off a higher percentage
of the vehicle value during the early
years of ownership. Accelerating these
tax deductions early on provides helpful
cash flow relief when new equipment
costs are highest. Section 179 provides
another powerful tax deduction tool for
qualifying commercial car owners and
fleet operators.
This tax provision lets businesses
deduct the full purchase price of
eligible new or used vehicles during the
tax year put into service. Heavy
vehicles with a gross vehicle weight
rating exceeding 6,000 lb often qualify
for substantial upfront write-offs.
Utilizing Section 179
allows growing companies to offset
immediate revenue with major equipment
investments. Bonus depreciation works
alongside standard tax deduction rules
to accelerate asset write-offs even
further for fleet owners.
This policy lets you deduct a percentage
of the vehicle cost in year one beyond
standard limit thresholds. While bonus
depreciation percentages change
according to federal legislation, it
remains a vital planning tool for major
fleet purchases.
Working with a qualified business
accountant ensures you take full
advantage of these evolving tax
incentives properly. Business vehicle
owners must choose between deducting
actual vehicle expenses or taking the
standard mileage rate deduction.
The actual expense method tracks
depreciation, fuel, repairs, insurance,
and maintenance costs together on your
tax return.
The standard mileage rate uses a flat
deduction rate per mile driven for
business purposes throughout the tax
year. For heavy commercial fleets,
tracking actual expenses usually yields
a larger overall tax write-off than
standard mileage calculations.
Deciding whether to lease or purchase
fleet vehicles comes down to how
depreciation impacts your tax structure.
Lease payments are generally fully
tax-deductible as operating expenses,
simplifying monthly accounting processes
significantly. Purchasing vehicles lets
you claim depreciation directly while
building asset equity on your corporate
balance sheet over time.
Analyzing your cash flow requirements
and tax bracket will reveal which
acquisition method fits your business
model.
Timing the resale or trade-in of your
fleet assets is critical to maximizing
financial recovery at cycle end. Selling
a vehicle right before major scheduled
maintenance services become due avoids
large out-of-pocket repair bills.
Aligning vehicle disposals with strong
seasonal beer demand in the secondary
market can net higher trade-in values.
Strategic timing ensures you exit an
asset right at the optimal point on its
depreciation curve. Avoiding common
accounting errors is essential when
managing commercial fleet vehicle
depreciation schedules over multiple
years.
Failing to recalculate residual values
after unexpected market shifts can leave
your financial statements inaccurate.
Misclassifying vehicle usage between
personal and commercial driving can also
trigger unnecessary tax audits and
penalties. Clean record-keeping and
regular asset reviews protect your
business from expensive accounting
surprises down the line.
Modern telematics and fleet tracking
software make tracking vehicle wear and
value loss easier than ever before.
These digital tools log real-time
mileage, driver habits, fuel
consumption, and maintenance alerts
automatically across all units. Having
access to continuous fleet data helps
management predict exact replacement
timelines before catastrophic breakdowns
occur.
Data-driven decisions prevent unexpected
asset write-downs while keeping fleet
operations completely predictable and
profitable.
Balancing operational cash flow with
long-term fleet depreciation requires
constant evaluation of your commercial
vehicle strategy. Upgrading vehicles too
quickly consumes valuable capital while
keeping aging vans too long leads to
soaring repair bills.
Finding the sweet spot where tax
deductions, low maintenance costs, and
high residual value meet keeps your
fleet financially healthy.
Continuous learning and proactive fleet
management ensure every vehicle in your
yard contributes directly to profit.
Understanding fleet vehicle asset
depreciation and tax write-offs gives
your business a huge competitive
advantage.
Proper asset management keeps your
overhead low and protects your
hard-earned revenue month after month.
Thanks for watching the video. Subscribe
to this channel. Like the video if you
found the video great. And if you have
any questions, leave me your comment
through the comment section.

metadata.shortDescription:
FleetBold Car Rental Software Demo for Turo Hosts, Fleet Owners, and Car Rental Operators

In this video, we walk through the FleetBold Car Rental Module, a complete software solution that helps fleet owners launch and manage their own car rental business without needing custom development or third-party booking platforms.

With FleetBold, you can create your own branded car rental website, publish vehicle listings, accept direct bookings, process payments with Stripe, manage guests, send rental agreements for e-signature, offer insurance and protection plans, complete vehicle inspections, and run your rental operation from one dashboard.



FleetBold is designed to help you own your brand, own your customer relationships, and grow beyond marketplace dependency.

If you are looking for car rental software, Turo host software, fleet management software, or a way to build your own private rental business, this demo will show you how FleetBold works.

Learn more about FleetBold and see how it can help power your rental operation.

1. What is FleetBold?
FleetBold is an all-in-one software platform for hosts, fleet operators, and private rental businesses that want to manage operations, bookings, guests, payments, websites, and vehicles from one place.

2. Can FleetBold help me run a private rental business?
Yes. FleetBold includes the core tools needed to operate a private rental business, including bookings, calendar, guest management, payments, insurance workflows, rental agreements, inspections, and website tools.

3. Can I manage bookings inside FleetBold?
Yes. FleetBold includes a dedicated bookings system so operators can manage reservations, workflows, and rental activity from one dashboard.

4. Does FleetBold include a reservation calendar?
Yes. FleetBold includes a calendar designed to help operators manage reservations, availability, and fleet planning more efficiently.

5. Can I create rental agreements inside FleetBold?
Yes. FleetBold includes rental agreement tools so you can manage agreements as part of your operation instead of relying on disconnected systems.

6. Does FleetBold include guest management?
Yes. FleetBold includes guest management tools to help you keep customer-related workflows organized inside the same platform.

7. Can I manage payments inside FleetBold?
Yes. FleetBold includes payment-related workflows as part of the rental operation, helping you centralize more of your business in one system.

8. Does FleetBold include vehicle inspections?
Yes. FleetBold includes vehicle inspection tools to help support check-in, check-out, and operational documentation workflows.

9. Can I build my own website with FleetBold?
Yes. FleetBold includes a website module that allows operators to build a branded online presence directly inside the platform.

10. Can I use my own custom domain?
Yes. FleetBold supports branded website workflows that are built for operators who want a more professional and independent online presence.

11. Does FleetBold help me generate my own traffic?
Yes. FleetBold is built not only to help you operate your business, but also to help you grow it. With your own website, you can control your traffic, promote your listings, and build your own marketing flow instead of only waiting for bookings.

12. Can I run ads to my website or listing?
Yes. FleetBold’s website tools are built for operators who want to drive traffic through platforms like Facebook and Google while maintaining more control over their brand and visibility.

13. Does FleetBold include analytics?
Yes. FleetBold includes analytics tools that help you understand website activity, user behavior, and performance inside your own system.

14. Can I connect Google Analytics?
Yes. FleetBold makes it easy to connect Google Analytics so you can go deeper into your website traffic and performance.

15. Can I connect Meta Pixel?
Yes. FleetBold supports growth-focused website workflows, including tools that help you control traffic and improve your advertising performance.

16. Does FleetBold include maintenance tools?
Yes. FleetBold includes a dedicated maintenance system designed to help operators manage service workflows, recurring needs, and vehicle readiness more efficiently.

17. Can FleetBold support larger operations?
Yes. FleetBold is built to support everything from smaller operators to more advanced multi-vehicle and multi-fleet businesses that need structure and scalability.

18. What makes FleetBold different from other rental software?
Most tools solve only one part of the business. FleetBold brings together rental operations, fleet control, agreements, inspections, websites, analytics, maintenance, and growth tools in one platform.

metadata.shortDescription:
Limo Anywhere is the Booking and Management software the big Livery, Black Car, and Limo companies use to run their operations and most Uber Black Drivers  don't even know they exist. In the episode of "Fares and Frustrations", I breakdown what Lime Anywhere actually is, how it works, and why it matters if you are trying to build a real Black Car business.

This is Part 1, the full explanation based on research and my conversation with the sales team. Part 2 will go deeper once I have purchased and set it up myself so I can show you exactly how it works in real time.

If you are a rideshare driver looking to upgrade to Uber Black or a Premier driver thinking about your next move, or you are already working with "Private" clients but tired of patching things together then this is the kind of software you need to know about.

Thanks for Watching! I do appreciate it. Don't forget to follow me on all other Social Media platforms as well. I am here to help.

segments.text: There's an entire layer of the
transportation business that Uber
drivers have no idea exist. We're out
here every day, heads down in the app,
chasing surges, watching the heat map,
and trying to get one more good ride
before we go home. And the whole time,
sitting right next to us at the same
airports, at the same hotels, and the
same corporate accounts, there's a
completely different world operating.
Real limo companies, real black car
services, real executive transportation
businesses, and almost all of them are
running on a piece of software that you
probably never heard of.
And it's called LimoAnywhere, and it's
been around for a while with almost
about 5,500 operators using it
worldwide. And it's basically the
operating system of the chauffeur
industry. And if you're serious about
building a private black car business
off the app, this is one of the most
important tools that you've never been
told about.
Now, let's start with the basics because
the name itself is a little misleading.
LimoAnywhere is not a marketplace. That
is the first thing that you got to
understand is it's not Uber, and it's
not Lyft. There is no pool of random
riders out there opening up LimoAnywhere
and looking for the closest driver or
requesting a ride. That world does not
exist. Nobody's going to find you on
LimoAnywhere who doesn't already know
who you are.
LimoAnywhere is a booking and management
platform built specifically for the
limo, black car, and chauffeur industry.
It's what's called a SaaS, software as a
service. You pay a monthly subscription,
and in return, you get the entire back
office of a transportation company in
one piece of software. And here is the
easiest way to think about it.
Uber is a marketplace. They bring you
the rider. They handle the booking, they
handle the payment, and they take a cut
out of every ride. Sometimes 50, 60, 70%
off the top. Limo anywhere, it's the
opposite. They don't bring you anybody.
You bring your own clients. From your
website, you bring them from your
business cards, from word of mouth, from
repeat customers, and from an affiliate
network that we'll talk about later. And
once you bring them in, the platform, it
handles everything after that. The
booking, the quote, the confirmation,
the payment, the dispatch, the receipt,
and the records. All of it. And you keep
100% of what you charge.
And that's the trade-off. Uber gives you
the customer, but takes most of the
money. Limo anywhere lets you keep all
the money, but you have to bring the
customer. That's the whole game right
there. The driver who figures out how to
bring their own customers are the ones
who graduate off the app. And this is
the platform that runs the business once
you start doing that.
Now, let me explain why this matters,
because I want you to feel the problem
before I tell you the solution. If
you've been watching this channel, you
know my whole thing is treating this
work like a business. The app is the
starting line, not the finish line. The
real money is in the private clients.
People who book you directly,
who become repeat customers, who refer
you to their friends, and who pay you
without Uber taking a chunk off the top.
But, here's what happens to most every
driver who tries to go in that
direction.
Now, you get that first private client.
Maybe it's a rider that you had off the
app who liked you. They asked you for
your number, and they want you for an
airport run next week. Cool. You text
back and forth. You You on a price. You
show up, and you do the ride. They pay
you on Cash App or Zelle. Easy, right?
Then it's two clients. Then it's five.
Then you start handing out business
cards, your website starts getting some
traffic, and now you got people emailing
you, texting you, calling you, all
wanting to book. And then it all falls
apart.
Then you miss a text. You double book on
a Saturday night because you didn't see
the email till the next day.
Somebody asked for a quote on a
Jacksonville to Orlando run, and you're
guessing every time. Somebody wants to
pay by credit card, and you don't have a
clean way to run it. Somebody wants a
receipt for their company to reimburse
them, and you're sending them a
screenshot from Cash App. Somebody asked
for a contract for a wedding, and you're
typing it up in Google Docs, and you're
hoping that it covers you. And then your
client lands at Jacksonville
International Airport. Their flight came
in 20 minutes early. You didn't even
know. And now they're standing there at
the curb texting you, wondering where
you are.
Now, this is the wall that every driver
who tries to build a private black car
service hits.
And most of them quit at this exact
point. Not because they couldn't get the
clients, but because they couldn't
manage the clients that they got. Limo
Anywhere is the answer to that wall.
Every single problem I just listed, that
double booking, the quoting, the credit
card processing, the receipts, the
contracts, the confirmations, and yes,
the flight tracking, that's exactly what
this platform was built to solve. It's
the difference between running a side
hustle out of your phone and running an
actual transportation company.
All right, let me walk you through how
this thing actually works in real life,
because the app situation is the part
that confused me at first also, and I
want to clear it up for you. I actually
had my meeting with these guys this
morning, so I'm going to break it down
on way they broke it down for me. There
are two pieces here. One is for you, the
operator, and then one is for your
client. They're not the same thing, and
neither one is a marketplace.
Now you got the operator app. That's
you. You log into on your phone or your
tablet. This is a command center. You
see every reservation that's been
booked, the calendar for the week, your
runs of the day. When a booking comes
in, it pops up here as a scheduled ride.
You tap it, you see the pickup, the
drop-off, the client name, some flight
info, special notes, payment status, and
you hit on the way. You hit arrived, you
hit passenger on board, and you hit trip
complete. Same flow you've already used
with the Uber driver app, except these
are bookings, your customers, and your
prices. You also see every reservation
in one place. Calendar view, daily run
sheet, the whole picture. When a client
books, it lands here. You see who, when,
where, what flight, and what they paid,
plus what's coming next.
Now I want to be straight with you. I
had my meeting with them this morning,
but they didn't walk me through every
single click of the operator app yet.
This is coming in part two when I do a
deeper dive. So I'm not going to sit
here and tell you exactly what every
button does because I haven't put my
hands on it myself. What I can tell you
is what the system is built to do, and
that it runs the back office of a
transportation company. From quote to
payment, to dispatch, to reporting, all
in one place.
Now this is the feature I want to spend
a minute on because this is the one that
got me sitting up in my chair during the
meeting. Because LimoAnywhere is
integrated with FlightAware and some
other tracking apps. So when a client
books an airport pickup and they put
their flight number in, the system
automatically tracks the flight in the
background. Every airport reservation,
every flight is tracked for you.
If their flight is delayed, the system
knows it. If their flight is early, the
system knows it.
You're not refreshing FlightAware on
your phone every 15 minutes.
You're not sitting in a cell phone lot
for an hour because a flight got pushed
back. You're not getting a panic text
because the flight came in early.
So, for a guy like me doing 20, 30
airport runs a month, that one feature
alone is worth a subscription.
I sat at JAX waiting on delayed flights
more times than I can count. This one
feature eliminates the guesswork on the
part of the job that wastes the most
time.
Now, let's say I have a repeat client
who's flying into Jacksonville. He pulls
up on my booking page on his phone,
the one he saved on his home screen from
my website. He picks a date, he picks
the vehicle, and he puts his flight
number in. The system calculates the
price automatically based on the rules
that I set up. His card's on file and it
gets pre-authorized, and he hits booked.
Within seconds, that booking lands in my
system. I see it on my schedule. The
flight tracking is already running. The
payment is already locked in. And I
didn't even have to text him back. I
didn't even have to quote a price. I
didn't have to send an invoice. I just
see the run on my schedule, and when
Tuesday comes around, I show up. And the
system already told me whether his
flight is on time, early, or delayed,
and before I even left the house. That's
the difference between running an actual
chauffeur business and running a side
hustle. Now, let me explain what the
rest of the platform does because the
booking flow and the flight tracking are
just a start. You got quoting and
pricing. You set the rates once, by the
hour, by the mile, by the zone, flat
rate to the airport, search multipliers
for holidays and peak times, whatever
pricing model that you want. The system
then applies them automatically. No more
pulling up Google Maps to figure out
what to charge somebody for a run to
Gainesville.
Then you have deposits and prepayment.
You can require deposit at booking, take
the full payment up front, or charge
after the ride. It's your call. The
system handles it either way.
Then you have dispatching and
rescheduling. Even as a one-car
operator, this matters. You see all your
up coming coming rides in one place.
When you grow to two or three cars, you
can assign rides to different drivers.
The system scales with you.
Then you got the flight tracking. Like I
just walked through, FlightAware is
integrated and every airport reservation
gets tracked automatically.
Then you got credit card processing,
integrated payments, card on file,
pre-authorization before the ride, and
charge after completion.
Tips, refunds, all of it through the
platform. No more Square card reader, no
more Cash App, no more chasing anybody
for payment.
Then you have customer accounts. Clients
have a portal where they could see their
ride history. They could save their
credit cards. They can rebook past trips
with just one click. And they can
request a quote. This is huge for repeat
business. The easier you make it to book
you again, the more they will. You have
an affiliate network. Now, this is the
part that most drivers don't even know
about, and it's a big deal. Limo
companies on the platform farm rides to
each other constantly. Somebody in
Atlanta books a round trip, but the
return leg is from Jacksonville. So,
they post it to the network, and if
you're on the platform, you can pick it
up. That's a whole revenue stream most
Uber drivers don't even know exist. And
you're getting paid by other limo
companies to handle their overflow in
your city.
Then you have reporting, revenue by the
month,
by the client, by the vehicle, by the
driver,
tax reports, profit and loss, the kind
of data that you actually need to run a
business.
Then you got integrations.
You got Stripe,
QuickBooks, Google Calendar, Outlook. It

already using. That's the platform, not
one feature, the whole back office of a

website or thinking about getting one.
I've got
fareswithoutthefrustrations.com.

That's three steps in a delay before any

That text link lives in your pocket for

Here's the part that matters. Your

positions you. But until you have a real

brochure. The minute you connect a

And the whole time, sitting right next to us at the same airports, at the same hotels, and the same corporate accounts, there's a completely different world operating. Real limo companies, real black car services, real executive transportation businesses, and almost all of them are running on a piece of software that you probably never heard of. And it's called LimoAnywhere, and it's been around for a while with almost about 5,500 operators using it worldwide. And it's basically the operating system of the chauffeur industry. And if you're serious about building a private black car business off the app, this is one of the most important tools that you've never been told about. Now, let's start with the basics because the name itself is a little misleading. LimoAnywhere is not a marketplace. That is the first thing that you got to understand is it's not Uber, and it's not Lyft. There is no pool of random riders out there opening up LimoAnywhere and looking for the closest driver or requesting a ride. That world does not exist. Nobody's going to find you on LimoAnywhere who doesn't already know who you are. LimoAnywhere is a booking and management platform built specifically for the limo, black car, and chauffeur industry. It's what's called a SaaS, software as a service. You pay a monthly subscription, and in return, you get the entire back office of a transportation company in one piece of software. And here is the easiest way to think about it. Uber is a marketplace. They bring you the rider. They handle the booking, they handle the payment, and they take a cut out of every ride. Sometimes 50, 60, 70% off the top. Limo anywhere, it's the opposite. They don't bring you anybody. You bring your own clients. From your website, you bring them from your business cards, from word of mouth, from repeat customers, and from an affiliate network that we'll talk about later. metadata.shortDescription:
See how Limo Anywhere connects dispatch, driver workflows, passenger communication, and pricing in this practical webinar featuring Taylor Latour and Brandon Edley.

Whether you're running a small black car service, managing a growing chauffeur fleet, or looking to get more from your existing Limo Anywhere software, this replay walks through real workflows you can put to use in your operation.

Follow a reservation from booking and dispatch to passenger updates, driver coordination, and post-trip feedback. Then explore how automation can reduce manual work and how Lead Quote Close can help turn more pricing inquiries into bookings.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

• Driver self-dispatch: See how drivers and owner-operators can create reservations and dispatch rides directly from the DriverAnywhere app.

• Passenger communication: Explore Passenger Link's live driver tracking, the Passenger Web App, and automated post-trip surveys.

• Custom Booking Portals: See how hotel concierges and other partners can book transportation through dedicated, branded portals.

• Driver Wake-Ups: Learn how automated reminders, calls, and escalation workflows can help manage early-morning pickups.

• Airport Passenger Assistance: Discover how automated messages can guide arriving passengers through luggage collection and pickup instructions.

• Lead Quote Close (LQC): Explore lead capture, automated quote follow-ups, marketing visibility, and flexible pricing using rate sheets, zones, and selection factors.

• Core, Plus & Black: Understand which Limo Anywhere capabilities are included in each subscription plan and where additional tools may fit your business.

WATCH, EXPLORE & TAKE THE NEXT STEP

Watch the webinar, jump directly to relevant demonstrations, explore related resources, or schedule a personalized walkthrough on our replay page:

https://www.limoanywhere.com/2026/10/21/from-dispatch-to-drop-off-limo-anywhere-webinar/

Compare Limo Anywhere Core, Plus & Black:
https://www.limoanywhere.com/pricing/

Request a personalized demo:
https://www.limoanywhere.com/book-a-demo/

ABOUT LIMO ANYWHERE

Limo Anywhere provides reservation, dispatch, driver management, passenger communication, and business management software for limousine, black car, chauffeur, and executive transportation operators.

From managing daily reservations to automating operational workflows and improving the booking experience, Limo Anywhere helps transportation businesses bring more of their work together.

Recorded November 5, 2026. Features and integrations shown reflect the software at the time of recording. Availability varies by plan and configuration.

metadata.title: Why Your Limo Business NEEDS Software to Scale (Stop Doing It the Old Way)
metadata.author: Luxury Transportation Academy / Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Think you don't need software to run a successful limo or black car business? Think again. 🚘💻

In this clip from The Luxury Transportation Podcast, Dr. Morris Parker (CEO of TCW Limo & founder of the Luxury Transportation Academy) breaks down why so many operators shy away from technology — and why that mindset is quietly capping their growth.

Dr. Parker shares his own journey adopting Limo Anywhere early in his career, treating new software like leveling up in a video game, and why "not being tech savvy" is never a real excuse in today's business landscape.

🎙️ In this episode, we cover:
✅ Why operators avoid new tech (and why that's a costly mistake)
✅ How Limo Anywhere helped scale a 6-figure limo business
✅ Why a CRM or even a simple email list can transform your growth
✅ The real day-to-day workflow of running a luxury transportation company — from 4am airport runs to nightly wrap-up
✅ How dispatch, maintenance, hiring, and marketing all fit into one system
✅ Why texting and WhatsApp are costing you data (and money)
✅ How to stop "figuring it out as you go" and build real operational structure

Whether you're a solo chauffeur just starting out or managing a growing fleet, this episode will show you why the right tech stack isn't optional — it's the difference between staying stuck and scaling to six figures and beyond.

📌 Want the full blueprint to grow your luxury transportation business? Learn more about the Luxury Transportation Academy (LTA) and get mentorship from operators who've already built it.

👉 Subscribe for new episodes of The Luxury Transportation Podcast every week!

#LuxuryTransportation #LimoBusiness #BlackCarService #ChauffeurLife #TechStack #LimoAnywhere #SmallBusinessGrowth #EntrepreneurPodcast #LTAAcademy #GroundTransportation
